**St. Joseph** is a city in and the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Buchanan County, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buchanan_County,_Missouri "Buchanan County, Missouri"), United States.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-GR6-4) Located on the [Missouri River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River"), it is the principal city of the [St. Joseph Metropolitan Statistical Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_Metropolitan_Statistical_Area "St. Joseph Metropolitan Statistical Area"), which includes [Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buchanan_County,_Missouri "Buchanan County, Missouri"), [Andrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_County,_Missouri "Andrew County, Missouri"), and [DeKalb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeKalb_County,_Missouri "DeKalb County, Missouri") counties in Missouri and [Doniphan County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doniphan_County,_Kansas "Doniphan County, Kansas"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas"). As of the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), St. Joseph had a population of 72,473,[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-Census2020PLLede-5) making it the [8th most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Missouri "List of cities in Missouri") in the state, and the 3rd most populous in Northwest Missouri.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-census-6) St. Joseph is located roughly 30 miles (48 km) north of the [Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri") city limits and approximately 125 miles (201 km) south of [Omaha, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaha,_Nebraska "Omaha, Nebraska").

The city was named after the town's founder [Joseph Robidoux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Robidoux_IV "Joseph Robidoux IV") and the biblical [Saint Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Joseph "Saint Joseph").[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-7) In the nineteenth century, it was the death place of American outlaw [Jesse James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_James "Jesse James"). It was also the starting point of the [Pony Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pony_Express "Pony Express") serving the West. Today, St. Joseph is home to [Missouri Western State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Western_State_University "Missouri Western State University"), which enrolls over 3,800 students.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-8)

## History

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Missouri&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 21](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/St_Joseph_Missouri_Francis.jpg/250px-St_Joseph_Missouri_Francis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Joseph_Missouri_Francis.jpg)

The intersection of Francis and North 4th streets in downtown St. Joseph

[![Image 22](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/St_Joseph_Missouri_River.jpg/250px-St_Joseph_Missouri_River.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Joseph_Missouri_River.jpg)

The [Missouri River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River") in St. Joseph

St. Joseph was founded on the Missouri River by [Joseph Robidoux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Robidoux_IV "Joseph Robidoux IV"), a local [fur trader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_trader "Fur trader") of French Canadian descent. It was officially incorporated in 1843.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-travel-9) In its early days, it was a bustling outpost and rough frontier town, serving as a last supply point and jumping-off point for travelers on the Missouri River toward the ["Wild West"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Old_West "American Old West"). It was the westernmost point in the United States accessible by rail until after the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), which helped earn it the designation "Gateway to the West."[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-10)

The main east–west downtown streets were named for Robidoux's eight children: Faraon, Jules, Francois (Francis), Felix, Edmond, Charles, Sylvanie, and Messanie. The street between Sylvanie and Messanie was named for his second wife, Angelique.

St. Joseph, or "St. Joe", as it was called by many, was a "Jumping-Off Point" for those migrants headed to the [Oregon Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Territory "Oregon Territory") in the mid-1800s. Such cities, including [Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence,_Missouri "Independence, Missouri"), and St. Joseph, were where pioneers would stay and purchase supplies before they headed out in wagon trains across the Great Plains. The town was a very lively place.

Between April 3, 1860, and late October 1861, St. Joseph was one of the two endpoints of the [Pony Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pony_Express "Pony Express"), which operated for a short period over the land then inaccessible by rail, to provide fast mail service. Today the [Pony Express Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pony_Express_Museum "Pony Express Museum") hosts visitors in the former stables of the company. St. Joseph is identified by the slogan, "Where the Pony Express started and Jesse James ended."

The town's main hotel was [Patee House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patee_House "Patee House"). In the post-Civil War years, when the economy was down, the hotel was used for a time by the Patee Female College. It was occupied by the [St. Joseph Female College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_Female_College "St. Joseph Female College") up to 1880.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-11)

In 1874 the State Lunatic Asylum #2[[12]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-12) was opened just East of St. Joseph. The asylum, originally built for 250 patients, opened its doors with more than 300. The asylum was mostly self-sustaining with three large farms, power plant, fire department, metal shops, wood shops, dairy and more, all worked by the patients. Over the decades the asylum grew rapidly, reaching its peak of close to 3,000 patients by the 1940s. In 1968 occupational therapist George Glore, with the help of his patients, recreated several historic treatment devices for Mental Health Awareness Month. This was the start of the [Glore Psychiatric Museum](https://www.stjosephmuseum.org/glore-psychiatric-museum). Now the largest museum of its kind in the world, the museum shows the history mental health treatment and still houses the original exhibits created by George Glore and his patients.

Outlaw [Jesse James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_James "Jesse James") lived here under the alias "Mr. Howard". The song, "[Jesse James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_James_(folk_song) "Jesse James (folk song)")", includes the lines, "...that dirty little coward that shot Mr. Howard has laid poor Jesse in his grave."[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-william-13) On April 3, 1882, James was killed at his home, originally located at 1318 Lafayette. It has been relocated next to the Patee House and still has the visible bullet hole from the fatal shot. It is now operated as the [Jesse James Home Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_James_Home_Museum "Jesse James Home Museum").

The Heaton-Bowman-Smith Funeral Home maintains a small museum about Jesse James. Their predecessors conducted his funeral.

St. Joseph was the second city in the US to install electric streetcars; regular service was initiated on July 4, 1888.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-14) Among properties listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") are [Robidoux Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robidoux_Row "Robidoux Row"), buildings owned by the founder and used for his family trading and mercantile business; the Patee House, now serving as a museum displaying St. Joseph's history, and the [Missouri Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Theater_and_Missouri_Theater_Building "Missouri Theater and Missouri Theater Building"), an ornate movie palace. The [Walnut Park Farm Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walnut_Park_Farm_Historic_District "Walnut Park Farm Historic District") near St. Joseph was listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") in 1999.[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-nris-15)

St. Joseph's population peaked in 1900, with a census population of 102,979. This population figure is questionable, as civic leaders were known to have tried to raise the numbers for that census.[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-bigcensus-16) At the time, Saint Joseph was home to one of the largest wholesale companies in the Midwest, the [Nave & McCord Mercantile Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nave_&_McCord_Mercantile_Company "Nave & McCord Mercantile Company"), as well as the [Hannibal and St. Joseph Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal_and_St._Joseph_Railroad "Hannibal and St. Joseph Railroad"), and the C.D. Smith & Company. C.D. Smith later became C.D. Smith Healthcare.

Prior to 1954 and desegregation, Bartlett High School served St. Joseph's African American students. It became Horace Mann Elementary with desegregation. You can learn about the Bartlett School at the [Black Archives Museum of St. Joseph](https://www.stjosephmuseum.org/black-archives-museum).[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-x798-17) St. Joseph's African American community leaders and [Nathaniel C. Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathaniel_C._Bruce "Nathaniel C. Bruce") were involved in and supported the establishment of [Bartlett Agricultural and Industrial School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartlett_Agricultural_and_Industrial_School "Bartlett Agricultural and Industrial School") in [Dalton, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalton,_Missouri "Dalton, Missouri"). It was modeled after [Tuskegee Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskegee_Institute "Tuskegee Institute") and [Hampton Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampton_Institute "Hampton Institute").

## Geography and climate

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Missouri&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography and climate")]

[![Image 24](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/St_Joseph_Missouri_skyline.jpg/330px-St_Joseph_Missouri_skyline.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Joseph_Missouri_skyline.jpg)

Another view of the downtown in 2006

Saint Joseph is located on the Missouri/[Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas") border in northwestern Missouri, also close to Nebraska; [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa "Iowa") is another 70 miles (110 km) farther north. The nearest major metropolitan area to St. Joseph is the [Kansas City Metropolitan Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_Metropolitan_Area "Kansas City Metropolitan Area"), which begins approximately 30 miles (48 km) to the south. The nearest major airport is [Kansas City International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_International_Airport "Kansas City International Airport"), which is approximately 35 miles (56 km) to the south. According to the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau"), the city has a total area of 44.77 square miles (115.95 km 2), of which 43.99 square miles (113.93 km 2) is land and 0.78 square miles (2.02 km 2) is water.[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-Gazetteer_files-18)

Several water bodies and streams are located in St. Joseph besides the Missouri River. [Roys Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roys_Branch "Roys Branch") sources just northwest of [Krug Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krug_Park_(St._Joseph,_Missouri) "Krug Park (St. Joseph, Missouri)") and travels southwest and enters the Missouri River next to Remington Nature Center. Whitehead Creek headwaters southeast of St. Joseph and flows northwest into the Missouri River just southwest of downtown. Corby Pond, a public lake in Corby Park, is a popular fishing location. [Lake Contrary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Contrary "Lake Contrary") is located just southwest of St. Joseph and has a beach.

Under the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"), St. Joseph has a [humid subtropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") (_Cfa_) bordering on a [humid continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") (_Dfa_), although under United States isotherms of 32°F (0°C) the station is firmly continental. The monthly weather averages listed below are taken from National Weather Service 1981–2010 normals recorded at Rosecrans Airport. Because of the airport's location near the Missouri River and at a low elevation, official overnight lows during wintertime especially are often several degrees colder than at other places within the city.[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-19) Snowfall is not recorded at the St. Joseph weather station although surrounding reporting stations typically receive 12 to 20 inches (0.30 to 0.51 meters) of snowfall annually.[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-20)[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-21)[[22]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-22)

## Business

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Missouri&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Business")]

St. Joseph has a vibrant and diversified industrial economy making it the third largest exporter in Missouri.[[33]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-33)[[34]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-34) The industry includes major food processing, research, development, and production facilities of animal health products. Production of a wide range of heavy equipment, bio-fuels, meat and grains processing, candies, food processing equipment, metal can production, along with two major general contractors.

At the center of the so-called 'Kansas City Animal Health Corridor', which extends from Manhattan, Kansas, to Columbia, Missouri, St. Joseph is home to major animal health, pharmaceutical, nutrition research facilities. Including Boehringer Ingelheim [[35]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-35) and Nestle Purina.[[36]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-36)

Other agricultural products including herbicides for crop production and retail are produced in St. Joseph.[[37]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-37)

Herzog is based in St. Joseph. [TransitAmerica Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TransitAmerica_Services "TransitAmerica Services"), a subsidiary of Herzog, provides conductors and other railway technical positions for transit rail systems nationwide. Herzog Contracting, parent company to Transit America, is based in the city and provides construction services, rail equipment, rail testing, and signaling services to freight and transit systems throughout North America and the Caribbean.[[38]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-38)[[39]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-39)

St. Joseph has the third-largest manufacturing economy in Missouri, after St. Louis and Kansas City.

In June 2019, total employment in the St. Joseph Metropolitan Area was 65,099 persons.[[40]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-40)

St. Joseph is home to several retail areas, many of which are grouped along Belt Highway on the city's east side. [East Hills Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Hills_Mall "East Hills Mall") is located at North Belt Highway and Frederick Boulevard. Developed in 2005, the Shoppes at North Village is concentrated along North Belt Highway between approximately Cook and County Line roads. Other shopping districts include Belt Center, Hy-Vee Shopping Center, Hillcrest Plaza, East Ridge Village, and Woodlawn Shopping Center.

## Education

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Missouri&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Education")]

### Public schools

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Missouri&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Public schools")]

The vast majority of the city limits is in the [St. Joseph School District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_School_District?action=edit&redlink=1 "St. Joseph School District (page does not exist)").[[42]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-CensusSDMap-42) The St. Joseph School District operates three public high schools, four public middle schools and 16 public elementary schools in St. Joseph. There are three private grade schools, a private high school and a private [K–12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-12_education "K-12 education") Christian school. Two new elementary schools (Oak Grove and Carden Park) have been constructed, and both opened by the 2014–15 academic year. In addition, there is an active home education community that serves the city and surrounding areas. In [higher education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education "Higher education"), St. Joseph is the home of a regional [public university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university") as well as a public university outreach center, a public [technical school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_school "Technical school") and a private technical school.

### Library

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Missouri&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Library")]

[![Image 27](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Free_Public_Library_at_St._Joseph%2C_Missouri.jpg/250px-Free_Public_Library_at_St._Joseph%2C_Missouri.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Free_Public_Library_at_St._Joseph,_Missouri.jpg)

Free Public Library at St. Joseph, Missouri

St. Joseph has a four-branch public library system.[[46]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-46)[[47]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-47) The system is overseen by the Library Board, which consists of nine members appointed by the mayor, with city council approval, for three-year terms.[[48]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-48) The [Downtown Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_Public_Library "St. Joseph Public Library"), located in downtown St. Joseph, houses the administrative offices for the library system.[[49]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-49)[Carnegie Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_Public_Library-Carnegie_Branch "St. Joseph Public Library-Carnegie Branch") and Washington Park Library are neighborhood branches that serve communities in the North and South ends of the city.[[50]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-50)[[51]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-51) East Hills Library is the largest branch, located off [Interstate 29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_29 "Interstate 29"), which serves the greater St. Joseph area.[[52]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-52) Downtown Library and Carnegie Library were listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") in 1982 and 1990 respectively.[[53]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-53)

St. Joseph also has a branch of the Rolling Hills Consolidated Library. This library was founded in 1961 with its headquarters in the basement of the Washington Park Library. The library currently occupies over 23,000 square feet of space off of the Belt Highway. The space is used for the library itself, its administration offices, a used book store, and "The Upper Story", a large rentable meeting room.[[54]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-:0-54)

A Burlington Northern passenger train at St. Joseph in 1970

The [St. Joseph Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_Transit "St. Joseph Transit") is publicly owned and provides bus service. [Rosecrans Memorial Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosecrans_Memorial_Airport "Rosecrans Memorial Airport") is a joint municipal/military owned airport for general aviation. It is the home of the [139th Airlift Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/139th_Airlift_Wing "139th Airlift Wing") of the [Missouri Air National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Air_National_Guard "Missouri Air National Guard"), and does not have commercial service. The nearest commercial airport is [Kansas City International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_International_Airport "Kansas City International Airport"), which is approximately 35 miles (56 km) to the south. Intercity bus service to the city is provided by [Jefferson Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Lines "Jefferson Lines").[[55]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-55)

## Cityscape

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Missouri&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Cityscape")]

Numerous parks, golf courses, sports complexes, skate parks, a water park, a [riverwalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedestrian_zone "Pedestrian zone") along the Missouri River, and a small conservation area can be found throughout St. Joseph proper. The city is also nationally known for its 26-mile (42 km)[parkway system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_Parkway "St. Joseph Parkway"), which is accompanied by an urban trail system.[[56]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-stjomo.com-56) Two of the city's largest parks are [Krug Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krug_Park_(St._Joseph,_Missouri) "Krug Park (St. Joseph, Missouri)") and Hyde Park; these respectively anchor the parkway and urban trail on the north and south. A [dog park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_park "Dog park") has been added to the parkway system near Corby Pond.[[57]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-57) There are many buildings that were built early on in the city's history, one of which being the [Missouri Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Theater_(St._Joseph,_Missouri) "Missouri Theater (St. Joseph, Missouri)").

## Media

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Missouri&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Media")]

St. Joseph currently ranks 201st largest [designated market area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Designated_market_area "Designated market area") out of 210 [media markets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_television_stations_in_North_America_by_media_market "List of television stations in North America by media market") in the United States (as ranked by [Nielsen Media Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_Media_Research "Nielsen Media Research")); the market covers six counties in northwestern Missouri ([Holt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holt_County,_Missouri "Holt County, Missouri"), [Worth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worth_County,_Missouri "Worth County, Missouri"), [Nodaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nodaway_County,_Missouri "Nodaway County, Missouri"), [Andrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_County,_Missouri "Andrew County, Missouri"), [DeKalb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeKalb_County,_Missouri "DeKalb County, Missouri") and [Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buchanan_County,_Missouri "Buchanan County, Missouri")) and [Doniphan County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doniphan_County,_Kansas "Doniphan County, Kansas") in northeastern Kansas. The St. Joseph area has three low-power and two full-power television stations, and ten radio stations. News-Press & Gazette, a media corporation, is headquartered in Saint Joseph. They have interests in numerous television, radio, and newspaper markets throughout the midwestern and western United States.[[58]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-58)

### Television

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Missouri&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Television")]

Due to its proximity to Kansas City, stations from that market serve as default affiliate of MyNetworkTV ([KSMO-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KSMO-TV "KSMO-TV")/Kansas City) and default member station of PBS ([KCPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KCPT "KCPT")/Kansas City) due to the lack of stations of either network licensed to the market. [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") affiliate [KQTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KQTV "KQTV") had long been the only major commercial station in St. Joseph, but in June 2012, the locally based [News-Press & Gazette Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News-Press_&_Gazette_Company "News-Press & Gazette Company") signed on [KNPN-LD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KNPN-LD "KNPN-LD") as a [Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Broadcasting_Company "Fox Broadcasting Company") affiliate, KBJO-LD as a [CW+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_CW_Plus "The CW Plus") affiliate, and KNPG-LD as a [Telemundo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telemundo "Telemundo") affiliate. This in turn was followed by the conversions of KBJO-LD to [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC") affiliate [KNPG-LD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KNPG-LD "KNPG-LD") in November 2016 (retaining the CW+ as a LD2 subchannel),[[59]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-newspress-knpgnbc-59) and the original KNPG-LD (which assumed the KBJO-LD call letters) to [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") affiliate [KCJO-LD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KCJO-LD "KCJO-LD") in June 2017,[[60]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri#cite_note-cbsstjoe-60) ending out-of-market reliance for major network programming.

**Jackson** is the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_capitals_in_the_United_States "List of capitals in the United States") and [most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Mississippi "List of municipalities in Mississippi") of the U.S. state of [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"). The city sits on the [Pearl River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_River_(Mississippi%E2%80%93Louisiana) "Pearl River (Mississippi–Louisiana)") and is located in the greater [Jackson Prairie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Prairie "Jackson Prairie") region of Mississippi. Along with [Raymond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond,_Mississippi "Raymond, Mississippi"), Jackson is one of two [county seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") for [Hinds County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinds_County,_Mississippi "Hinds County, Mississippi"). The city had a population of 153,701 at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), a decline of 11.42% from 173,514 since the [2010 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_census "2010 United States census"), representing the largest decline in population during the decade of any [major U.S. city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_cities_in_the_U.S. "Major cities in the U.S.").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-5) The [Jackson metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_metropolitan_area,_Mississippi "Jackson metropolitan area, Mississippi") is the largest metropolitan area located entirely in the state and the tenth-largest urban area in the [Deep South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_South "Deep South"), with 592,000 residents in 2020.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-metrojacksoneda.com-6)

The city is located in the Deep South halfway between [Memphis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee") and [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") on [Interstate 55](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_55 "Interstate 55") and [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas") and [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta") on [Interstate 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_20 "Interstate 20"). Founded in 1821 as the new state capital for Mississippi, Jackson is named after General [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson"), a war hero in the [Battle of New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_New_Orleans "Battle of New Orleans") during the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812") and subsequently the seventh U.S. president. Following the [Battle of Vicksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vicksburg "Battle of Vicksburg"), which was fought 45 miles west of Jackson during the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") in 1863, [Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(American_Civil_War) "Union (American Civil War)") forces commanded by General [William Tecumseh Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tecumseh_Sherman "William Tecumseh Sherman") launched the [siege of Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Expedition "Jackson Expedition") and set the city on fire.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-7) During the 1920s, Jackson surpassed [Meridian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian,_Mississippi "Meridian, Mississippi") to become the most populous city in the state following a speculative [natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas") boom in the region.

The slogan for Jackson is "The City with Soul".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-8) It has had numerous musicians prominent in [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music"), [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), and [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"). The city has a number of museums and cultural institutions, including the [Mississippi Children's Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Children's_Museum "Mississippi Children's Museum"), [Mississippi Museum of Natural Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Museum_of_Natural_Science "Mississippi Museum of Natural Science"), [Mississippi Civil Rights Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Civil_Rights_Museum "Mississippi Civil Rights Museum"), [Mississippi Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Museum_of_Art "Mississippi Museum of Art"), [Old Capital Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol "Old Mississippi State Capitol"), [Museum of Mississippi History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Mississippi_History "Museum of Mississippi History"). Other notable locations are the [Mississippi Coliseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Coliseum "Mississippi Coliseum") and the [Mississippi Veterans Memorial Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Veterans_Memorial_Stadium "Mississippi Veterans Memorial Stadium"), home of the [Jackson State Tigers football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_State_Tigers_football "Jackson State Tigers football") team. In 2020, the Jackson metropolitan area held a [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP") of $30 billion, accounting for 29% of the state's total GDP.

The entire [Choctaw Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choctaw "Choctaw")'s location and size compared to the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi")

### Founding and antebellum period (to 1860)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Founding and antebellum period (to 1860)")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Andrew_Jackson.jpg/250px-Andrew_Jackson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Andrew_Jackson.jpg)

[Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson"), the [7th President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States "List of presidents of the United States") and the city's namesake

The Jackson area was historically populated by the [Choctaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choctaw "Choctaw"), the majority of whom were forcibly [removed to Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trail_of_Tears "Trail of Tears") following Andrew Jackson's signing of the [Indian Removal Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Removal_Act "Indian Removal Act") in 1830.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-Howard_Zinn-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-Jackson_PBS-10) However, per the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, Choctaws could remain in Mississippi where they would be granted citizenship.

Located on the historic [Natchez Trace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natchez_Trace "Natchez Trace") trade route, the Choctaw town that stood where Jackson is today was called _Chisha Foka_, meaning "Among the [post oaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_oak "Post oak")."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-11) The city's first European American settler was Louis LeFleur, a [French-Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-Canadian "French-Canadian") trader. The village became known as [LeFleur's Bluff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeFleur's_Bluff "LeFleur's Bluff").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-jackhist-12) During the late 18th century and early 19th century, this site had a [trading post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_post "Trading post"). It was connected to markets in [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"). Soldiers returning to Tennessee from the military campaigns near [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") in 1815 built a public road that connected [Lake Pontchartrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Pontchartrain "Lake Pontchartrain") in Louisiana to this district.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-13) A United States treaty with the Choctaw, the [Treaty of Doak's Stand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Doak's_Stand "Treaty of Doak's Stand") in 1820, formally opened the area for non-Native American settlers.

LeFleur's Bluff was developed when it was chosen as the site for the new state's [capital city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city"). The [Mississippi General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Legislature "Mississippi Legislature") decided in 1821 that the state needed a centrally located capital (the legislature was then located in [Natchez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natchez,_Mississippi "Natchez, Mississippi")). They commissioned [Thomas Hinds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hinds "Thomas Hinds"), James Patton, and William Lattimore to look for a suitable site. The absolute center of the state was a swamp, so the group had to widen their search.

After surveying areas north and east of Jackson, they proceeded southwest along the [Pearl River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_River_(Mississippi%E2%80%93Louisiana) "Pearl River (Mississippi–Louisiana)") until they reached LeFleur's Bluff in today's Hinds County.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-jackhist-12) Their report to the General Assembly stated that this location had beautiful and healthful surroundings, good water, abundant timber, navigable waters, and proximity to the [Natchez Trace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natchez_Trace "Natchez Trace"). The Assembly passed an act on November 28, 1821, authorizing the site as the permanent seat of the government of the state of Mississippi.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-jackhist-12) On the same day, it passed a resolution to instruct the [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") delegation to press [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") for a donation of public lands on the river for improved navigation to the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-14) One [Whig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whig_Party_(United_States) "Whig Party (United States)") politician lamented the new capital as a "serious violation of principle" because it was not at the absolute center of the state.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-15)

The capital was named for General [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson"), to honor his January 1815 victory at the [Battle of New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_New_Orleans "Battle of New Orleans") during the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812"). He was later elected as the seventh [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States").

The city of Jackson was originally planned, in April 1822, by [Peter Aaron Van Dorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Aaron_Van_Dorn "Peter Aaron Van Dorn") in a "[checkerboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkerboard "Checkerboard")" pattern advocated by [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-ancestrypeter-16)[City blocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_block "City block") alternated with parks and other open spaces. Over time, many of the park squares have been [developed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate_development "Real estate development") rather than maintained as [green space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_open_space "Urban open space"). The state legislature first met in Jackson on December 23, 1822. In 1839, the Mississippi Legislature passed the first state law in the U.S. to permit married women to own and administer their own property.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-17)

Jackson was connected by public road to [Vicksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicksburg,_Mississippi "Vicksburg, Mississippi") and [Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton,_Mississippi "Clinton, Mississippi") in 1826.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-18) Jackson was first connected by railroad to other cities in 1840. An 1844 map shows Jackson linked by an east–west rail line running between Vicksburg, [Raymond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond,_Mississippi "Raymond, Mississippi"), and [Brandon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon,_Mississippi "Brandon, Mississippi"). Unlike Vicksburg, [Greenville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenville,_Mississippi "Greenville, Mississippi"), and [Natchez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natchez,_Mississippi "Natchez, Mississippi"), Jackson is not located on the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"), and it did not develop into a much larger city during the [antebellum era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antebellum_era "Antebellum era") as those cities did from major river commerce. The construction of railroad lines to the city sparked its growth in the decades following the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").

### American Civil War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: American Civil War")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Jacksonsiege1863.jpg/250px-Jacksonsiege1863.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jacksonsiege1863.jpg)

September 1863 map of the siege of Jackson

Despite its small population, during the Civil War, Jackson became a strategic center of manufacturing for the [Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America"). In 1863, during the military campaign which ended in the [capture of Vicksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Vicksburg "Siege of Vicksburg"), [Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(American_Civil_War) "Union (American Civil War)") forces captured Jackson during two battles—once before the fall of Vicksburg and once after the fall of Vicksburg.

On May 14, 1863, Union forces won the first [Battle of Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Jackson,_Mississippi "Battle of Jackson, Mississippi"), forcing [Confederate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_Army "Confederate States Army") forces to flee northward towards [Canton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Mississippi "Canton, Mississippi"). On May 14, Union troops under the command of [William Tecumseh Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tecumseh_Sherman "William Tecumseh Sherman") burned and looted key facilities in Jackson, a strategic manufacturing and railroad center for the Confederacy.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-JB-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-20) After driving the Confederate forces out of Jackson, Union forces turned west and engaged the Vicksburg defenders at the [Battle of Champion Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Champion_Hill "Battle of Champion Hill") in nearby [Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards,_Mississippi "Edwards, Mississippi"). The Union forces began their siege of Vicksburg soon after their victory at Champion Hill. Confederate forces began to reassemble in Jackson in preparation for an attempt to break through the Union lines surrounding Vicksburg and end the siege. The Confederate forces in Jackson built defensive [fortifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortification "Fortification") encircling the city while preparing to march west to Vicksburg.

Confederate forces marched out of Jackson in early July 1863 to break the siege of Vicksburg. But, unknown to them, Vicksburg had already surrendered on July 4, 1863. General [Ulysses S. Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant "Ulysses S. Grant") dispatched General Sherman to meet the Confederate forces heading west from Jackson. Upon learning that Vicksburg had already surrendered, the Confederates retreated into Jackson. Union forces began the [siege of Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jackson "Siege of Jackson"), which lasted for approximately one week. Union forces encircled the city and began an [artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery "Artillery") bombardment. One of the Union artillery emplacements has been preserved on the grounds of the [University of Mississippi Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Mississippi_Medical_Center "University of Mississippi Medical Center") in Jackson. [John C. Breckinridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Breckinridge "John C. Breckinridge"), former United States [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States"), served as one of the Confederate generals defending Jackson. On July 16, 1863, Confederate forces slipped out of Jackson during the night and retreated across the Pearl River.

Union forces completely burned the city after its capture this second time. The city was called "Chimneyville" because only the chimneys of houses were left standing.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-JB-19) The northern line of Confederate defenses in Jackson during the siege was located along a road near downtown Jackson, now known as Fortification Street.

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Jackson-StarsAndStripesHarpers.jpg/330px-Jackson-StarsAndStripesHarpers.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackson-StarsAndStripesHarpers.jpg)

Engraving from _[Harper's Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper's\_Weekly "Harper's Weekly")_, June 20, 1863, after the capture of Jackson by Union forces during the American Civil War

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Jackson_December_2018_37_%28Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol%29.jpg/250px-Jackson_December_2018_37_%28Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackson_December_2018_37_(Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol).jpg)

[Mississippi Old Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol "Old Mississippi State Capitol"), downtown Jackson

Because of the siege and following destruction, few [antebellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antebellum_architecture "Antebellum architecture") structures have survived in Jackson. The [Governor's Mansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Governor's_Mansion "Mississippi Governor's Mansion"), built in 1842, served as Sherman's headquarters and has been preserved. Another is the [Old Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol "Old Mississippi State Capitol") building, which served as the home of the Mississippi state legislature from 1839 to 1903. The Mississippi legislature passed the ordinance of [secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession") from the Union there on January 9, 1861, becoming the second state to secede from the United States. The [Jackson City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_City_Hall "Jackson City Hall"), built in 1846 for less than $8,000, also survived. It is said that Sherman, a [Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freemasonry "Freemasonry"), spared it because it housed a [Masonic Lodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masonic_Lodge "Masonic Lodge"), though a more likely reason is that it housed an army hospital.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-21) Additionally, the Manship House (Ca. 1857) survives.

### Reconstruction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Reconstruction")]

During [Reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_Era "Reconstruction Era"), African Americans were granted civil rights. Schools were established and African Americans held political offices. [Eugene Welborne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Welborne "Eugene Welborne"), [Charles Reese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Reese_(politician) "Charles Reese (politician)"), [Weldon Hicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weldon_Hicks "Weldon Hicks"), and [George Caldwell Granberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Caldwell_Granberry "George Caldwell Granberry") were among the legislators who represented Hinds County in the legislature. African Americans also served in local offices, as judges, and as marshalls.

Mississippi had considerable insurgent action, as whites struggled to maintain white supremacy. Jackson's appointed mayor [Joseph G. Crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_G._Crane "Joseph G. Crane") was stabbed to death in 1869. The assailant, [Edward M. Yerger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_M._Yerger "Edward M. Yerger"), was arrested by military authorities but, after a U.S. Supreme Court case ([Ex parte Yerger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex_parte_Yerger "Ex parte Yerger")), he was bonded out, moved to Baltimore and was never tried.

The economic recovery from the Civil War was slow through the start of the 20th century, but there were some developments in transportation. In 1871, the city introduced mule-drawn streetcars which ran on State Street, which were replaced by electric ones in 1899.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-22) In 1875, the [Red Shirts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Shirts_(United_States) "Red Shirts (United States)") were formed, one of the second waves of insurgent [paramilitary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramilitary "Paramilitary") organizations that essentially operated as "the military arm of the Democratic Party" to take back political power from the Republicans and to drive black people from the polls ([Mississippi Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Plan "Mississippi Plan")).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-23)

### Post-Reconstruction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Post-Reconstruction")]

Democrats regained control of the state legislature in 1876. The constitutional convention of 1890, which produced Mississippi's Constitution of 1890, was held at the capitol.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-OC-24) This was the first of new constitutions or amendments ratified in each Southern state through 1908 that effectively [disenfranchised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disenfranchisement_after_the_Reconstruction_Era "Disenfranchisement after the Reconstruction Era") most [African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") and many poor whites, through provisions making voter registration more difficult: such as [poll taxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poll_taxes_in_the_United_States "Poll taxes in the United States"), residency requirements, and [literacy tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy_test "Literacy test"). These provisions survived a Supreme Court challenge in 1898.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-26) As 20th-century Supreme Court decisions later ruled such provisions were unconstitutional, Mississippi and other Southern states rapidly devised new methods to continue disfranchisement of most black people, who comprised a majority in the state until the 1930s. Their exclusion from politics was maintained into the late 1960s.

The so-called [New Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_State_Capitol "Mississippi State Capitol") replaced the older structure upon its completion in 1903. Today the Old Capitol is operated as a historical museum.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-OC-24)
