Author [Eudora Welty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eudora_Welty "Eudora Welty") was born in Jackson in 1909, lived most of her life in the Belhaven section of the city, and died there in 2001. Her [memoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memoir "Memoir") of development as a writer, _[One Writer's Beginnings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One\_Writer's\_Beginnings "One Writer's Beginnings")_ (1984), presented a picture of the city in the early 20th century. She won the [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize") in 1973 for her novel, _[The Optimist's Daughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Optimist's\_Daughter "The Optimist's Daughter"),_ and is best known for her novels and short stories. The main library of the [Jackson/Hinds Library System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson/Hinds_Library_System "Jackson/Hinds Library System") was named in her honor,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-27) and her home has been designated as a [National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark").

[Richard Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Wright_(author) "Richard Wright (author)"), a highly acclaimed African-American author, lived in Jackson as an adolescent and young man in the 1910s and 1920s. He related his experience in his memoir _[Black Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Boy "Black Boy")_ (1945). He described the harsh and largely terror-filled life most African Americans experienced in the South and Northern ghettos such as [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago") under [segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States "Racial segregation in the United States") in the early 20th century.

Jackson had significant growth in the early 20th century, which produced dramatic changes in the city's skyline. Jackson's new [Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_(Jackson,_Mississippi) "Union Station (Jackson, Mississippi)") downtown reflected the city's service by multiple rail lines, including the [Illinois Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Central "Illinois Central").

Across the street, the new, luxurious [King Edward Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Edward_Hotel_(Jackson,_Mississippi) "King Edward Hotel (Jackson, Mississippi)") opened its doors in 1923, having been built according to a design by New Orleans architect [William T. Nolan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_T._Nolan "William T. Nolan"). It became a center for prestigious events held by Jackson society and Mississippi politicians. Nearby, the 18-story [Standard Life Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Life_Building "Standard Life Building"), designed in 1929 by Claude Lindsley, was the largest reinforced concrete structure in the world upon its completion.

Jackson's economic growth was further stimulated in the 1930s by the discovery of [natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas") fields nearby. Speculators had begun searching for oil and natural gas in Jackson beginning in 1920. The initial drilling attempts came up empty. This failure did not stop Ella Render from obtaining a lease from the state's insane asylum to begin a well on its grounds in 1924, where he found natural gas. (Render eventually lost the rights when courts determined that the asylum did not have the right to lease the state's property.) Businessmen jumped on the opportunity and dug wells in the Jackson area. The continued success of these ventures attracted further investment. By 1930, there were 14 derricks in the Jackson skyline.

Mississippi Governor [Theodore Bilbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Bilbo "Theodore Bilbo") stated:

> It is no idle dream to prophesy that the state's share [of the oil and natural gas profits] properly safe-guarded would soon pay the state's entire bonded indebtedness and even be great enough to defray all the state's expenses and make our state tax free so long as obligations are concerned.

This enthusiasm was subdued when the first wells failed to produce oil of a sufficiently high gravity for commercial success. The barrels of oil had considerable amounts of saltwater, which lessened the quality. The governor's prediction was wrong in hindsight, but the oil and natural gas industry did provide an economic boost for the city and state. The effects of the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") were mitigated by the industry's success. At its height in 1934, there were 113 producing wells in the state. The overwhelming majority were closed by 1955.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-28)

Due to provisions in the federal [Rivers and Harbors Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rivers_and_Harbors_Act "Rivers and Harbors Act"), on October 25, 1930, city leaders met with U.S. Army engineers to ask for federal help to alleviate Jackson flooding.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-29) J.J. Halbert, city engineer, proposed a straightening and dredging of the [Pearl River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_River_(Mississippi%E2%80%93Louisiana) "Pearl River (Mississippi–Louisiana)") below Jackson.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-30)

#### Jackson's Gold Coast

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Jackson's Gold Coast")]

During Mississippi's extended [Prohibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prohibition_in_the_United_States "Prohibition in the United States") period, from the 1920s until the 1960s, illegal drinking and gambling casinos flourished on the east side of the Pearl River, in [Flowood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowood,_Mississippi "Flowood, Mississippi") along with the original [U.S. Route 80](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_80 "U.S. Route 80") just across from the city of Jackson. Those illegal casinos, bootleg liquor stores, and nightclubs made up the Gold Coast, a strip of mostly [black-market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black-market "Black-market") businesses that operated for decades along Flowood Road. Although outside the law, the Gold Coast was a thriving center of nightlife and music, with many local blues musicians appearing regularly in the clubs.

The Gold Coast declined and businesses disappeared after Mississippi's prohibition laws were repealed in 1966, allowing Hinds County, including Jackson, to go "wet".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-31) In addition, [integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_integration "Racial integration") drew off business from establishments that earlier had catered to African Americans, such as the [Summers Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summers_Hotel_and_Subway_Lounge "Summers Hotel and Subway Lounge"). When it opened in 1943 on Pearl Street, it was one of two hotels in the city that served black clients. For years its Subway Lounge was a prime performance spot for black musicians playing jazz and blues.

In another major change, in 1990 the state-approved gaming on riverboats.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-32) Numerous casinos have been developed on riverboats, mostly in [Mississippi Delta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Delta "Mississippi Delta") towns such as [Tunica Resorts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunica_Resorts "Tunica Resorts"), [Greenville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenville,_Mississippi "Greenville, Mississippi"), and [Vicksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicksburg,_Mississippi "Vicksburg, Mississippi"), as well as [Biloxi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biloxi,_Mississippi "Biloxi, Mississippi") on the [Gulf Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Coast_of_the_United_States "Gulf Coast of the United States"). Before the damage and losses due to [Hurricane Katrina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Katrina "Hurricane Katrina") in 2005, the state ranked second nationally in gambling revenues[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_].

#### World War II and later development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: World War II and later development")]

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), [Hawkins Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkins_Field_(airport) "Hawkins Field (airport)") (at that time, also known as the Jackson Army Airbase) the American 21st, 309th, and 310th Bomber Groups that were stationed at the base were re-deployed for combat.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-33) Following the [German invasion of the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Netherlands "Battle of the Netherlands") and the [Japanese invasion of the Dutch East Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_Indies_campaign "Dutch East Indies campaign"), between 688 and 800 members of the Dutch Airforce escaped to the UK or Australia for training and, out of necessity, were eventually given permission by the United States to make use of Hawkins Field.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-34)

From May 1942 until the end of the war, all Dutch military aircrews trained at the base and went on to serve in either the British or Australian Air Forces.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-35)

In 1949, the poet [Margaret Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Walker "Margaret Walker") began teaching at [Jackson State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_State_University "Jackson State University"), a [historically black college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_college "Historically black college"). She taught there until 1979 and founded the university's Center for African-American Studies. Her poetry collection won a [Yale Younger Poets Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Younger_Poets_Prize "Yale Younger Poets Prize"). Her second novel, _[Jubilee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee\_(Walker\_novel) "Jubilee (Walker novel)")_ (1966), is considered a major work of African-American literature. She has influenced many younger writers.

### Civil rights movement in Jackson

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Civil rights movement in Jackson")]

The [civil rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement "Civil rights movement") had been active for decades, particularly mounting legal challenges to Mississippi's constitution and laws that disfranchised black people. Beginning in 1960, Jackson as the state capital became the site for dramatic non-violent protests in a new phase of activism that brought in a wide variety of participants in the performance of mass demonstrations.

In 1960, the U.S. Census Bureau reported Jackson's population as 64.3% white and 35.7% black.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-census1-36) At the time, public facilities were segregated and [Jim Crow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Crow "Jim Crow") was in effect. Efforts to [desegregate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desegregation_in_the_United_States "Desegregation in the United States") Jackson facilities began when nine [Tougaloo College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tougaloo_College "Tougaloo College") students tried to read books in the "white only" public library and were arrested. Founded as a [historically black college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_college "Historically black college") (HBCU) by the [American Missionary Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Missionary_Association "American Missionary Association") after the Civil War, [Tougaloo College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tougaloo_College "Tougaloo College") helped organize both black and white students of the region to work together for civil rights. It created partnerships with the neighboring mostly white [Millsaps College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millsaps_College "Millsaps College") to work with student activists. It has been recognized as a site on the "Civil Rights Trail" by the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-37)

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Jackson_December_2018_20_%28Old_Greyhound_Bus_Station%29.jpg/250px-Jackson_December_2018_20_%28Old_Greyhound_Bus_Station%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackson_December_2018_20_(Old_Greyhound_Bus_Station).jpg)

[Old Greyhound Bus Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Greyhound_Bus_Station_(Jackson,_Mississippi) "Old Greyhound Bus Station (Jackson, Mississippi)")

The mass demonstrations of the 1960s were initiated with the arrival of more than 300 [Freedom Riders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_Riders "Freedom Riders") on May 24, 1961. They were arrested in Jackson for [disturbing the peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breach_of_the_peace "Breach of the peace") after they disembarked from their interstate buses. The interracial teams rode the buses from [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), and sat together to demonstrate against segregation on public transportation, as the Constitution provides for unrestricted public transportation.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-38) Although the Freedom Riders had intended [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") as their final destination, Jackson was the farthest that any managed to travel. New participants kept joining the movement, as they intended to fill the jails in Jackson with their protest. The riders had encountered extreme violence along the way, including a bus burning and physical assaults. They attracted national media attention to the struggle for constitutional rights.

After the Freedom Rides, students and activists of the Freedom Movement launched a series of merchant [boycotts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boycott "Boycott"),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-39) sit-ins and protest marches,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-40) from 1961 to 1963. Businesses discriminated against black customers. For instance, at the time, department stores did not hire black salesclerks or allow black customers to use their fitting rooms to try on clothes, or lunch counters for meals while in the store, but they wanted them to shop in their stores.

In Jackson, shortly after midnight on June 12, 1963, [Medgar Evers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medgar_Evers "Medgar Evers"), civil rights activist and leader of the Mississippi chapter of the [NAACP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAACP "NAACP"), was assassinated by [Byron De La Beckwith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byron_De_La_Beckwith "Byron De La Beckwith"), a [white supremacist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacist "White supremacist") associated with the [White Citizens' Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Citizens'_Council "White Citizens' Council"). Thousands marched in Evers' funeral procession to protest the killing.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-41) Two trials at the time both resulted in [hung juries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hung_jury "Hung jury"). A portion of [U.S. Highway 49](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Highway_49 "U.S. Highway 49"), all of Delta Drive, a library, the central post office for the city, and [Jackson–Evers International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson%E2%80%93Evers_International_Airport "Jackson–Evers International Airport") were named in honor of Medgar Evers. In 1994, prosecutors Ed Peters and [Bobby DeLaughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_DeLaughter "Bobby DeLaughter") finally obtained a murder conviction in a state trial of De La Beckwith based on new evidence.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-42)

During 1963 and 1964, civil rights organizers gathered residents for voter education and [voter registration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voter_registration "Voter registration"). Black people had been essentially disfranchised since 1890. In a pilot project in 1963, activists rapidly registered 80,000 voters across the state, demonstrating the desire of African Americans to vote. In 1964 they created the [Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Freedom_Democratic_Party "Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party") as an alternative to the all-white state Democratic Party, and sent an alternate slate of candidates to the national Democratic Party convention in [Atlantic City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_City,_New_Jersey "Atlantic City, New Jersey"), New Jersey, that year.

Segregation and the disfranchisement of African Americans gradually ended after the Civil Rights Movement gained Congressional passage of the [Civil Rights Act of 1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964 "Civil Rights Act of 1964") and [Voting Rights Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_Rights_Act "Voting Rights Act") of 1965. In June 1966, Jackson was the terminus of the James Meredith March, organized by [James Meredith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith "James Meredith"), the first [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American "African American") to enroll at the [University of Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Mississippi "University of Mississippi"). The march, which began in [Memphis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee"), Tennessee, was an attempt to garner support for full implementation of civil rights in practice, following the legislation. It was accompanied by a new drive to register African Americans to vote in Mississippi. In this latter goal, it succeeded in registering between 2,500 and 3,000 black Mississippians to vote. The march ended on June 26 after Meredith, who had been wounded by a sniper's bullet earlier on the march, addressed a large rally of some 15,000 people in Jackson.

In September 1967 a [Ku Klux Klan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan "Ku Klux Klan") chapter bombed the synagogue of the [Beth Israel Congregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregation_Beth_Israel_(Jackson,_Mississippi) "Congregation Beth Israel (Jackson, Mississippi)") in Jackson, and in November bombed the house of its rabbi, Dr. [Perry Nussbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregation_Beth_Israel_(Jackson,_Mississippi)#Perry_Nussbaum_era "Congregation Beth Israel (Jackson, Mississippi)").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-BethIsrael-43) He and his congregation had supported civil rights.

Gradually the old barriers came down. Since that period, both whites and [Black Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Americans "Black Americans") in the state have had a consistently high rate of voter registration and turnout. Following the decades of the [Great Migration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Migration_(African_American) "Great Migration (African American)"), when more than one million black people left the rural South, since the 1930s the state has been majority white in total population. African Americans are a majority in the city of Jackson, although the metropolitan area is majority white. African Americans are also a majority in several cities and counties of the [Mississippi Delta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Delta "Mississippi Delta"), which are included in the [2nd congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi's_2nd_congressional_district "Mississippi's 2nd congressional district").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-44) The other three congressional districts are majority white.

### Mid-1960s to present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Mid-1960s to present")]

The first successful cadaveric [lung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lung "Lung")[transplant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_transplantation "Organ transplantation") was performed at the [University of Mississippi Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Mississippi_Medical_Center "University of Mississippi Medical Center") in Jackson in June 1963 by Dr. [James Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hardy_(surgeon) "James Hardy (surgeon)"). Hardy transplanted the cadaveric lung into a patient suffering from lung cancer. The patient survived for eighteen days before dying of [kidney failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidney_failure "Kidney failure").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-45)

In 1966 it was estimated that recurring flood damage at Jackson from the Pearl River averaged nearly a million dollars per year. The [U.S. Army Corps of Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army_Corps_of_Engineers "U.S. Army Corps of Engineers") spent $6.8 million on [levees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levee "Levee") and a new channel in 1966 before the project completion to prevent a flood equal to the December 1961 event plus an additional foot.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-46)

Since 1968, Jackson has been the home of [Malaco Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaco_Records "Malaco Records"), one of the leading record companies for [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music"), [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), and [soul music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") in the United States. In January 1973, [Paul Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Simon "Paul Simon") recorded the songs "Learn How to Fall" and "Take Me to the Mardi Gras", found on the album _[There Goes Rhymin' Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/There\_Goes\_Rhymin'\_Simon "There Goes Rhymin' Simon")_, in Jackson at the Malaco Recording Studios. Many well-known Southern artists recorded on the album, including the [Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscle_Shoals_Rhythm_Section "Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section") (David Hood, Jimmy Johnson, Roger Hawkins, Barry Beckett), [Carson Whitsett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carson_Whitsett "Carson Whitsett"), the [Onward Brass Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onward_Brass_Band "Onward Brass Band") from New Orleans, and others. The label has recorded many leading soul and blues artists, including [Bobby Bland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Bland "Bobby Bland"), [ZZ Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZZ_Hill "ZZ Hill"), [Latimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latimore_(musician) "Latimore (musician)"), [Shirley Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Brown "Shirley Brown"), [Denise LaSalle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denise_LaSalle "Denise LaSalle"), and [Tyrone Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrone_Davis "Tyrone Davis").

On May 15, 1970, [Jackson police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Police_Department_(Mississippi) "Jackson Police Department (Mississippi)") killed two students and wounded twelve at [Jackson State College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_State_University "Jackson State University") after a protest of the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") included students' overturning and burning some cars. These killings occurred eleven days after the [National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Guard_of_the_United_States "National Guard of the United States") killed four students in an anti-war protest at [Kent State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_State_University "Kent State University") in [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio"), and were part of national social unrest.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-47)_[Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek "Newsweek")_ cited the Jackson State killings in its issue of May 18 when it suggested that U.S. President [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon") faced a new [home front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_front "Home front").

The influx of illegal drugs occurred nationally as smugglers used the highways, seaports, and airports of the Gulf region.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-49) The 1980s in Jackson were dominated by Mayor [Dale Danks Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dale_Danks "Dale Danks") until he was unseated by lawyer and legislator [J. Kane Ditto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Kane_Ditto "J. Kane Ditto"), who criticized the deficit funding and the politicized police department of the city.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-50) Federal investigations of drug trafficking at Jackson's [Hawkins Field airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkins_Field_(airport) "Hawkins Field (airport)") were a part of the _Kerry Report,_ the 1986 U.S. Senate investigation of public corruption and foreign relations.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-51)

As Jackson has become the medical and legal center of the state, it has attracted [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") professionals in both fields. Since the late 20th century, it has developed the largest [Jewish community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Jews "American Jews") in the state.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-52)

In 1997, [Harvey Johnson, Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Johnson,_Jr. "Harvey Johnson, Jr.") was elected as Jackson's first African-American mayor. During his term, he proposed the development of a [convention center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_center "Convention center") to attract more business to the city. In 2004, during his second term, 66 percent of the voters passed a referendum for a tax to build the Convention Center.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-53)

Mayor Johnson was replaced by [Frank Melton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Melton "Frank Melton") on July 4, 2005. Melton generated controversy through his unconventional behavior, which included acting as a law enforcement officer. A dramatic spike in crime ensued during his term, despite Melton's efforts to reduce crime. The lack of jobs contributed to climb.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-54) In 2006 a young African-American businessman, Starsky Darnell Redd, was convicted of [money laundering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_laundering "Money laundering") in federal court along with his mother, other associates, and Billy Tucker, the former airport security chief.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-55)

In 2007, [Hinds County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinds_County,_Mississippi "Hinds County, Mississippi") sheriff Malcolm McMillin was appointed as the new police chief in Jackson, setting a historic precedent. McMillin was both the [county sheriff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_sheriff "County sheriff") and city police chief until 2009, when he stepped down due to disagreements with the mayor. Mayor Frank Melton died in May 2009, and City Councilman Leslie McLemore served as acting mayor of Jackson until July 2009, when former Mayor Harvey Johnson was elected and assumed the position.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-56)

On June 26, 2011, 49-year-old [James Craig Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_James_Craig_Anderson "Murder of James Craig Anderson") was killed in Jackson after being beaten, robbed, and run over by a group of white teenagers. The district attorney described it as a "[hate crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_crime "Hate crime")", and the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI "FBI") investigated it as a civil rights violation.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-Sperling-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-Severson0822-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-ap0822-59)

On March 18, 2013, a severe [hailstorm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail "Hail") hit the Jackson metro area. The hail caused major damage to roofs, vehicles, and building siding. Hail ranged in size from golfball to softball. There were more than 40,000 hailstorm claims of homeowner and automobile damage.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-61)

In 2013, Jackson was named as one of the top 10 friendliest cities in the United States by _CN Traveler_. The capital city was tied with [Natchez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natchez,_Mississippi "Natchez, Mississippi") as Number 7. The city was noticed for friendly people, great food, and green and pretty public places.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-62)

On July 1, 2013, [Chokwe Lumumba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chokwe_Lumumba "Chokwe Lumumba") was sworn into office as mayor of the city. After eight months in office, Lumumba died on February 25, 2014. Lumumba was a popular yet controversial figure due to his prior membership in the [Republic of New Afrika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_New_Afrika "Republic of New Afrika"), as well as being a co-founder of the [National Coalition of Blacks for Reparations in America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Coalition_of_Blacks_for_Reparations_in_America "National Coalition of Blacks for Reparations in America").

Lumumba's son, [Chokwe Antar Lumumba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chokwe_Antar_Lumumba "Chokwe Antar Lumumba"), ran for the mayoral seat following his father's death, but lost to Councillor [Tony Yarber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Yarber "Tony Yarber") on April 22, 2014.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-63) In 2017, however, Chokwe Antar Lumumba ran for mayor again, and won. Following his victory, on June 26 he was interviewed by Amy Goodman on _[Democracy Now!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy\_Now! "Democracy Now!")_,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-64) at which time he declared a commitment to make Jackson the "Most Radical City on the Planet".

For several years, the city water supply failed to meet [federal drinking water standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe_Drinking_Water_Act#National_Primary_Drinking_Water_Regulations "Safe Drinking Water Act") and was subject to many [boil water orders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boil_water_order "Boil water order") in 2021 and 2022. Due to deteriorating water infrastructure, some parts of the city experienced low water pressure, and in some neighborhoods residents reported untreated sewage flowing in city streets.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-65) In August 2022, Jackson [lost access to water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi_water_crisis "Jackson, Mississippi water crisis") when its largest water treatment plant failed, leaving tap water untreated.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-66)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Jackson_Mississippi.jpg/250px-Jackson_Mississippi.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackson_Mississippi.jpg)

Photograph of Jackson Mississippi taken from the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station")

The city of Jackson is located primarily in northeastern Hinds County. Jackson also includes around 3,000 acres (12.1 km 2) in [Rankin County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankin_County,_Mississippi "Rankin County, Mississippi") comprising [Jackson-Medgar Evers International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson%E2%80%93Medgar_Wiley_Evers_International_Airport "Jackson–Medgar Wiley Evers International Airport") and a small portion of [Madison County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_County,_Mississippi "Madison County, Mississippi"). The [Pearl River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_River_(Mississippi%E2%80%93Louisiana) "Pearl River (Mississippi–Louisiana)") forms most of the eastern border of the city. A small portion of the city containing [Tougaloo College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tougaloo_College "Tougaloo College") is the portion of Jackson that lies in Madison County, bounded on the west by [Interstate 220](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_220_(Mississippi) "Interstate 220 (Mississippi)") and on the east by the [U.S. Route 51](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_51 "U.S. Route 51") and [Interstate 55](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_55 "Interstate 55"). In the 2010 census, only 622 of the city's residents lived in Madison County,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-67) and only 1 lived within the city limits in Rankin County.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-68) The city is bordered to the north by [Ridgeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridgeland,_Mississippi "Ridgeland, Mississippi") in Madison County, to the northeast by [Ross Barnett Reservoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Barnett_Reservoir "Ross Barnett Reservoir") on the Pearl River, to the east by [Flowood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowood,_Mississippi "Flowood, Mississippi") and [Richland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richland,_Mississippi "Richland, Mississippi") in Rankin County, to the south by [Byram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byram,_Mississippi "Byram, Mississippi") in Hinds County, and to the west by [Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton,_Mississippi "Clinton, Mississippi") in Hinds County.

According to the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau"), the city has a total area of 113.2 square miles (293.3 km 2), of which 111.0 square miles (287.6 km 2) are land and 2.2 square miles (5.7 km 2), or 1.94% of the total, are water.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-Census_2010-69)

### Cityscape

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Cityscape")]

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Downtown_Jackson_June_2020.jpg/500px-Downtown_Jackson_June_2020.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Downtown_Jackson_June_2020.jpg)

Downtown Jackson is situated directly on the banks of the Pearl River. The downtown district has direct connections to both Interstate 55 via Pearl Street and Pasagoula Street and Interstate 20 via State Street (US 51). Much of the downtown was constructed before the 1980s and only small additions to the skyline have been made since then.

### Geology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Geology")]

For the most part, Jackson is built on acidic, variably drained silt loam [soil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil "Soil"). [Loess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loess "Loess") forms the topsoil in western sections, where the Loring soil series is common. The Tippo series, also a silt loam, is found in the central flood plain. Farther east, common soil series include Guyton silt loam, Providence silt loam and Smithdale fine sandy loam.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-70)

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Jackson_gas_wells_map.png/250px-Jackson_gas_wells_map.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackson_gas_wells_map.png)

Jackson structure map

Jackson sits atop the extinct [Jackson Volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Volcano "Jackson Volcano"), located 2,900 feet (880 m) underground. It is the only capital city in the United States to have this feature. The buried peak of the volcano is located directly below the [Mississippi Coliseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Coliseum "Mississippi Coliseum").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-Jackson_Volcano-71) The municipality is drained on the west by tributaries of the [Big Black River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Black_River_(Mississippi) "Big Black River (Mississippi)") and on the east by the Pearl River, which is 150 feet (46 m) higher than the Big Black near [Canton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Mississippi "Canton, Mississippi"). The artesian groundwater flow is not as extensive in Jackson for this reason. The first large-scale well was drilled in the city in 1896, and the city water supply has relied on surface water resources.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-72)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Climate")]

Jackson is located in the [humid subtropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") zone ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification")_Cfa_). Rain occurs throughout the year, though the winter and spring are the wettest seasons, while September and October are usually the driest months. Snow is rare, and accumulation very seldom lasts more than a day.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-NCDC-73) Average annual precipitation is 57.35 inches (1,457 mm), see climate table.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-74) Much of Jackson's rainfall occurs during thunderstorms. Thunder is heard on roughly 70 days each year. Jackson lies in a region prone to [severe thunderstorms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severe_thunderstorm "Severe thunderstorm") which can produce large [hail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail "Hail"), damaging winds, and [tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado"). Among the most notable tornado events was the F5 [Candlestick Park tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_Park_tornado "Candlestick Park tornado") on March 3, 1966, which destroyed the shopping center of the same name and surrounding businesses and residential areas, killing 19 in South Jackson.

The record low temperature is −5°F (−21°C), set on January 27, 1940,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-NOWData_Jackson,_MS-75) and the record high is 107°F (42°C), recorded on September 6–7, 1925, July 29, 1930, and August 30, 2000.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-NOWData_Jackson,_MS-75)

Jackson remained a small town for much of the 19th century. Before the American Civil War, Jackson's population remained small, particularly in contrast to the river towns along the commerce-laden [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"). Despite the city's status as the state capital, the 1850 census only counted 1,881 residents, excluding slaves, which were not separately enumerated.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-81)

By 1900, the population of Jackson was still less than 8,000. Although it expanded rapidly, during this period [Meridian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian,_Mississippi "Meridian, Mississippi") became Mississippi's largest city, based on trade, manufacturing, and access to transportation via railroad and highway.

In the early 20th century, Jackson had its largest rates of growth but ranked second to Meridian in Mississippi. By 1944, Jackson's population had risen to some 70,000 inhabitants, and it became the largest city in the state. For several decades, Jackson had the most thriving business districts and the largest public school system in Mississippi.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-82)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-83) It achieved its peak population in the 1980 census of more than 200,000 residents in the city. Since 1980, Jackson has declined in population due to several factors while its surrounding [suburban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburban "Suburban") population has increased.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-84)

**Jackson** is the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_capitals_in_the_United_States "List of capitals in the United States") and [most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Mississippi "List of municipalities in Mississippi") of the U.S. state of [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"). The city sits on the [Pearl River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_River_(Mississippi%E2%80%93Louisiana) "Pearl River (Mississippi–Louisiana)") and is located in the greater [Jackson Prairie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Prairie "Jackson Prairie") region of Mississippi. Along with [Raymond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond,_Mississippi "Raymond, Mississippi"), Jackson is one of two [county seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") for [Hinds County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinds_County,_Mississippi "Hinds County, Mississippi"). The city had a population of 153,701 at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), a decline of 11.42% from 173,514 since the [2010 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_census "2010 United States census"), representing the largest decline in population during the decade of any [major U.S. city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_cities_in_the_U.S. "Major cities in the U.S.").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-5) The [Jackson metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_metropolitan_area,_Mississippi "Jackson metropolitan area, Mississippi") is the largest metropolitan area located entirely in the state and the tenth-largest urban area in the [Deep South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_South "Deep South"), with 592,000 residents in 2020.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-metrojacksoneda.com-6)

The city is located in the Deep South halfway between [Memphis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee") and [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") on [Interstate 55](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_55 "Interstate 55") and [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas") and [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta") on [Interstate 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_20 "Interstate 20"). Founded in 1821 as the new state capital for Mississippi, Jackson is named after General [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson"), a war hero in the [Battle of New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_New_Orleans "Battle of New Orleans") during the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812") and subsequently the seventh U.S. president. Following the [Battle of Vicksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vicksburg "Battle of Vicksburg"), which was fought 45 miles west of Jackson during the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") in 1863, [Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(American_Civil_War) "Union (American Civil War)") forces commanded by General [William Tecumseh Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tecumseh_Sherman "William Tecumseh Sherman") launched the [siege of Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Expedition "Jackson Expedition") and set the city on fire.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-7) During the 1920s, Jackson surpassed [Meridian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian,_Mississippi "Meridian, Mississippi") to become the most populous city in the state following a speculative [natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas") boom in the region.

The slogan for Jackson is "The City with Soul".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-8) It has had numerous musicians prominent in [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music"), [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), and [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"). The city has a number of museums and cultural institutions, including the [Mississippi Children's Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Children's_Museum "Mississippi Children's Museum"), [Mississippi Museum of Natural Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Museum_of_Natural_Science "Mississippi Museum of Natural Science"), [Mississippi Civil Rights Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Civil_Rights_Museum "Mississippi Civil Rights Museum"), [Mississippi Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Museum_of_Art "Mississippi Museum of Art"), [Old Capital Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol "Old Mississippi State Capitol"), [Museum of Mississippi History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Mississippi_History "Museum of Mississippi History"). Other notable locations are the [Mississippi Coliseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Coliseum "Mississippi Coliseum") and the [Mississippi Veterans Memorial Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Veterans_Memorial_Stadium "Mississippi Veterans Memorial Stadium"), home of the [Jackson State Tigers football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_State_Tigers_football "Jackson State Tigers football") team. In 2020, the Jackson metropolitan area held a [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP") of $30 billion, accounting for 29% of the state's total GDP.

### Founding and antebellum period (to 1860)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Founding and antebellum period (to 1860)")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Andrew_Jackson.jpg/250px-Andrew_Jackson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Andrew_Jackson.jpg)

[Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson"), the [7th President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States "List of presidents of the United States") and the city's namesake

The Jackson area was historically populated by the [Choctaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choctaw "Choctaw"), the majority of whom were forcibly [removed to Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trail_of_Tears "Trail of Tears") following Andrew Jackson's signing of the [Indian Removal Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Removal_Act "Indian Removal Act") in 1830.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-Howard_Zinn-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-Jackson_PBS-10) However, per the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, Choctaws could remain in Mississippi where they would be granted citizenship.

Located on the historic [Natchez Trace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natchez_Trace "Natchez Trace") trade route, the Choctaw town that stood where Jackson is today was called _Chisha Foka_, meaning "Among the [post oaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_oak "Post oak")."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-11) The city's first European American settler was Louis LeFleur, a [French-Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-Canadian "French-Canadian") trader. The village became known as [LeFleur's Bluff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeFleur's_Bluff "LeFleur's Bluff").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-jackhist-12) During the late 18th century and early 19th century, this site had a [trading post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_post "Trading post"). It was connected to markets in [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"). Soldiers returning to Tennessee from the military campaigns near [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") in 1815 built a public road that connected [Lake Pontchartrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Pontchartrain "Lake Pontchartrain") in Louisiana to this district.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-13) A United States treaty with the Choctaw, the [Treaty of Doak's Stand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Doak's_Stand "Treaty of Doak's Stand") in 1820, formally opened the area for non-Native American settlers.

LeFleur's Bluff was developed when it was chosen as the site for the new state's [capital city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city"). The [Mississippi General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Legislature "Mississippi Legislature") decided in 1821 that the state needed a centrally located capital (the legislature was then located in [Natchez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natchez,_Mississippi "Natchez, Mississippi")). They commissioned [Thomas Hinds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hinds "Thomas Hinds"), James Patton, and William Lattimore to look for a suitable site. The absolute center of the state was a swamp, so the group had to widen their search.

After surveying areas north and east of Jackson, they proceeded southwest along the [Pearl River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_River_(Mississippi%E2%80%93Louisiana) "Pearl River (Mississippi–Louisiana)") until they reached LeFleur's Bluff in today's Hinds County.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-jackhist-12) Their report to the General Assembly stated that this location had beautiful and healthful surroundings, good water, abundant timber, navigable waters, and proximity to the [Natchez Trace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natchez_Trace "Natchez Trace"). The Assembly passed an act on November 28, 1821, authorizing the site as the permanent seat of the government of the state of Mississippi.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-jackhist-12) On the same day, it passed a resolution to instruct the [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") delegation to press [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") for a donation of public lands on the river for improved navigation to the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-14) One [Whig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whig_Party_(United_States) "Whig Party (United States)") politician lamented the new capital as a "serious violation of principle" because it was not at the absolute center of the state.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-15)

The capital was named for General [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson"), to honor his January 1815 victory at the [Battle of New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_New_Orleans "Battle of New Orleans") during the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812"). He was later elected as the seventh [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States").

The city of Jackson was originally planned, in April 1822, by [Peter Aaron Van Dorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Aaron_Van_Dorn "Peter Aaron Van Dorn") in a "[checkerboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkerboard "Checkerboard")" pattern advocated by [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-ancestrypeter-16)[City blocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_block "City block") alternated with parks and other open spaces. Over time, many of the park squares have been [developed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate_development "Real estate development") rather than maintained as [green space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_open_space "Urban open space"). The state legislature first met in Jackson on December 23, 1822. In 1839, the Mississippi Legislature passed the first state law in the U.S. to permit married women to own and administer their own property.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-17)

Jackson was connected by public road to [Vicksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicksburg,_Mississippi "Vicksburg, Mississippi") and [Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton,_Mississippi "Clinton, Mississippi") in 1826.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-18) Jackson was first connected by railroad to other cities in 1840. An 1844 map shows Jackson linked by an east–west rail line running between Vicksburg, [Raymond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond,_Mississippi "Raymond, Mississippi"), and [Brandon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon,_Mississippi "Brandon, Mississippi"). Unlike Vicksburg, [Greenville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenville,_Mississippi "Greenville, Mississippi"), and [Natchez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natchez,_Mississippi "Natchez, Mississippi"), Jackson is not located on the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"), and it did not develop into a much larger city during the [antebellum era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antebellum_era "Antebellum era") as those cities did from major river commerce. The construction of railroad lines to the city sparked its growth in the decades following the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").

### American Civil War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: American Civil War")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Jacksonsiege1863.jpg/250px-Jacksonsiege1863.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jacksonsiege1863.jpg)

September 1863 map of the siege of Jackson

Despite its small population, during the Civil War, Jackson became a strategic center of manufacturing for the [Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America"). In 1863, during the military campaign which ended in the [capture of Vicksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Vicksburg "Siege of Vicksburg"), [Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(American_Civil_War) "Union (American Civil War)") forces captured Jackson during two battles—once before the fall of Vicksburg and once after the fall of Vicksburg.

On May 14, 1863, Union forces won the first [Battle of Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Jackson,_Mississippi "Battle of Jackson, Mississippi"), forcing [Confederate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_Army "Confederate States Army") forces to flee northward towards [Canton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Mississippi "Canton, Mississippi"). On May 14, Union troops under the command of [William Tecumseh Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tecumseh_Sherman "William Tecumseh Sherman") burned and looted key facilities in Jackson, a strategic manufacturing and railroad center for the Confederacy.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-JB-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-20) After driving the Confederate forces out of Jackson, Union forces turned west and engaged the Vicksburg defenders at the [Battle of Champion Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Champion_Hill "Battle of Champion Hill") in nearby [Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards,_Mississippi "Edwards, Mississippi"). The Union forces began their siege of Vicksburg soon after their victory at Champion Hill. Confederate forces began to reassemble in Jackson in preparation for an attempt to break through the Union lines surrounding Vicksburg and end the siege. The Confederate forces in Jackson built defensive [fortifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortification "Fortification") encircling the city while preparing to march west to Vicksburg.

Confederate forces marched out of Jackson in early July 1863 to break the siege of Vicksburg. But, unknown to them, Vicksburg had already surrendered on July 4, 1863. General [Ulysses S. Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant "Ulysses S. Grant") dispatched General Sherman to meet the Confederate forces heading west from Jackson. Upon learning that Vicksburg had already surrendered, the Confederates retreated into Jackson. Union forces began the [siege of Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jackson "Siege of Jackson"), which lasted for approximately one week. Union forces encircled the city and began an [artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery "Artillery") bombardment. One of the Union artillery emplacements has been preserved on the grounds of the [University of Mississippi Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Mississippi_Medical_Center "University of Mississippi Medical Center") in Jackson. [John C. Breckinridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Breckinridge "John C. Breckinridge"), former United States [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States"), served as one of the Confederate generals defending Jackson. On July 16, 1863, Confederate forces slipped out of Jackson during the night and retreated across the Pearl River.

Union forces completely burned the city after its capture this second time. The city was called "Chimneyville" because only the chimneys of houses were left standing.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-JB-19) The northern line of Confederate defenses in Jackson during the siege was located along a road near downtown Jackson, now known as Fortification Street.

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Jackson-StarsAndStripesHarpers.jpg/330px-Jackson-StarsAndStripesHarpers.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackson-StarsAndStripesHarpers.jpg)

Engraving from _[Harper's Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper's\_Weekly "Harper's Weekly")_, June 20, 1863, after the capture of Jackson by Union forces during the American Civil War

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Jackson_December_2018_37_%28Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol%29.jpg/250px-Jackson_December_2018_37_%28Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackson_December_2018_37_(Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol).jpg)

[Mississippi Old Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol "Old Mississippi State Capitol"), downtown Jackson

Because of the siege and following destruction, few [antebellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antebellum_architecture "Antebellum architecture") structures have survived in Jackson. The [Governor's Mansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Governor's_Mansion "Mississippi Governor's Mansion"), built in 1842, served as Sherman's headquarters and has been preserved. Another is the [Old Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Mississippi_State_Capitol "Old Mississippi State Capitol") building, which served as the home of the Mississippi state legislature from 1839 to 1903. The Mississippi legislature passed the ordinance of [secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession") from the Union there on January 9, 1861, becoming the second state to secede from the United States. The [Jackson City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_City_Hall "Jackson City Hall"), built in 1846 for less than $8,000, also survived. It is said that Sherman, a [Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freemasonry "Freemasonry"), spared it because it housed a [Masonic Lodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masonic_Lodge "Masonic Lodge"), though a more likely reason is that it housed an army hospital.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-21) Additionally, the Manship House (Ca. 1857) survives.

### Reconstruction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Reconstruction")]

During [Reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_Era "Reconstruction Era"), African Americans were granted civil rights. Schools were established and African Americans held political offices. [Eugene Welborne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Welborne "Eugene Welborne"), [Charles Reese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Reese_(politician) "Charles Reese (politician)"), [Weldon Hicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weldon_Hicks "Weldon Hicks"), and [George Caldwell Granberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Caldwell_Granberry "George Caldwell Granberry") were among the legislators who represented Hinds County in the legislature. African Americans also served in local offices, as judges, and as marshalls.

Mississippi had considerable insurgent action, as whites struggled to maintain white supremacy. Jackson's appointed mayor [Joseph G. Crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_G._Crane "Joseph G. Crane") was stabbed to death in 1869. The assailant, [Edward M. Yerger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_M._Yerger "Edward M. Yerger"), was arrested by military authorities but, after a U.S. Supreme Court case ([Ex parte Yerger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex_parte_Yerger "Ex parte Yerger")), he was bonded out, moved to Baltimore and was never tried.

The economic recovery from the Civil War was slow through the start of the 20th century, but there were some developments in transportation. In 1871, the city introduced mule-drawn streetcars which ran on State Street, which were replaced by electric ones in 1899.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-22) In 1875, the [Red Shirts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Shirts_(United_States) "Red Shirts (United States)") were formed, one of the second waves of insurgent [paramilitary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramilitary "Paramilitary") organizations that essentially operated as "the military arm of the Democratic Party" to take back political power from the Republicans and to drive black people from the polls ([Mississippi Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Plan "Mississippi Plan")).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-23)

### Post-Reconstruction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackson,_Mississippi&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Post-Reconstruction")]

Democrats regained control of the state legislature in 1876. The constitutional convention of 1890, which produced Mississippi's Constitution of 1890, was held at the capitol.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-OC-24) This was the first of new constitutions or amendments ratified in each Southern state through 1908 that effectively [disenfranchised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disenfranchisement_after_the_Reconstruction_Era "Disenfranchisement after the Reconstruction Era") most [African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") and many poor whites, through provisions making voter registration more difficult: such as [poll taxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poll_taxes_in_the_United_States "Poll taxes in the United States"), residency requirements, and [literacy tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy_test "Literacy test"). These provisions survived a Supreme Court challenge in 1898.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-26) As 20th-century Supreme Court decisions later ruled such provisions were unconstitutional, Mississippi and other Southern states rapidly devised new methods to continue disfranchisement of most black people, who comprised a majority in the state until the 1930s. Their exclusion from politics was maintained into the late 1960s.

The so-called [New Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_State_Capitol "Mississippi State Capitol") replaced the older structure upon its completion in 1903. Today the Old Capitol is operated as a historical museum.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi#cite_note-OC-24)
