The **Saint Joseph River** (known locally as the **Saint Joe**) is a 210-mile-long (340 km)[river](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River "River") that flows in a generally westerly direction through [southern Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Michigan "Southern Michigan") and [northern Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Indiana "Northern Indiana"), United States, before emptying into [Lake Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Michigan "Lake Michigan"). The Saint Joseph River [drainage basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") covers 4,685 square miles (12,130 km 2), and is the third largest watershed draining to Lake Michigan. The land within its bounds is primarily used for [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture"). The river and its tributaries provide a variety of [paddling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddling "Paddling") and fishing environments. Historically, the river served as an important [canoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canoe "Canoe") transportation route for various [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") tribes, and for [French Canadian Voyageurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyageurs "Voyageurs").

## Description of the watershed

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description of the watershed")]

The Saint Joseph River watershed drains 4,685 square miles (12,130 km 2) from 15 counties: [Berrien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_County,_Michigan "Berrien County, Michigan"), [Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branch_County,_Michigan "Branch County, Michigan"), [Calhoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calhoun_County,_Michigan "Calhoun County, Michigan"), [Cass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_Michigan "Cass County, Michigan"), [Hillsdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsdale_County,_Michigan "Hillsdale County, Michigan"), [Kalamazoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalamazoo_County,_Michigan "Kalamazoo County, Michigan"), [Saint Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_County,_Michigan "St. Joseph County, Michigan") and [Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Buren_County,_Michigan "Van Buren County, Michigan") in Michigan and [DeKalb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeKalb_County,_Indiana "DeKalb County, Indiana"), [Elkhart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elkhart_County,_Indiana "Elkhart County, Indiana"), [Kosciusko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosciusko_County,_Indiana "Kosciusko County, Indiana"), [LaGrange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaGrange_County,_Indiana "LaGrange County, Indiana"), [Noble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_County,_Indiana "Noble County, Indiana"), [Saint Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_County,_Indiana "St. Joseph County, Indiana") and [Steuben](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steuben_County,_Indiana "Steuben County, Indiana") in Indiana. The watershed includes 3,742 river miles (6,022 km) and flows through and near the Kalamazoo-Portage, Elkhart-Goshen, Mishawaka-South Bend, and Saint Joseph/Benton Harbor metropolitan areas.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-WMP-5) The St. Joseph River main stem is 206 miles (332 km) long, rising in southern Michigan in [Hillsdale County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsdale_County,_Michigan "Hillsdale County, Michigan") flowing from [Baw Beese Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baw_Beese_Lake "Baw Beese Lake"), within 5 miles (8 km) of the headwaters of the other Saint Joseph River of the eastward-flowing [Maumee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maumee_River "Maumee River") watershed. Baw Beese Lake was historically named for the [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi") Chief [Baw Beese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baw_Beese "Baw Beese").

The river follows a zigzag route generally westward across southern Michigan, dipping into northern Indiana. From its headwaters, it flows initially northwest past [Hillsdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsdale,_Michigan "Hillsdale, Michigan") into southeastern [Calhoun County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calhoun_County,_Michigan "Calhoun County, Michigan"), then turns abruptly southwest to flow past [Tekonsha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekonsha,_Michigan "Tekonsha, Michigan"), [Union City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_City,_Michigan "Union City, Michigan"), [Sherwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherwood,_Michigan "Sherwood, Michigan"), and [Mendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendon,_Michigan "Mendon, Michigan"). At [Three Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Rivers,_Michigan "Three Rivers, Michigan") it is joined from the north by the [Rocky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_River_(Michigan) "Rocky River (Michigan)") and [Portage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portage_River_(St._Joseph_County) "Portage River (St. Joseph County)") rivers, and by the [Prairie River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prairie_River_(Michigan) "Prairie River (Michigan)") from the east, after making an abrupt turn south. At [Constantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine,_Michigan "Constantine, Michigan") it receives the [Fawn River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fawn_River_(Michigan) "Fawn River (Michigan)") from the east. Next, after returning to a southwest course, it receives the [Pigeon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeon_River_(St._Joseph_River)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pigeon River (St. Joseph River) (page does not exist)") from the east, near the Michigan–[Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana") state line. In northern Indiana, the river flows west-southwest through [Elkhart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elkhart,_Indiana "Elkhart, Indiana"), [Mishawaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mishawaka "Mishawaka"), and South Bend, where it turns abruptly north to re-enter southwestern Michigan in southeastern [Berrien County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_County,_Michigan "Berrien County, Michigan"). In southwestern Michigan, it follows a wide [meandering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meander "Meander") route generally northwest through [Niles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niles,_Michigan "Niles, Michigan") and past [Berrien Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_Springs,_Michigan "Berrien Springs, Michigan"). Just North of Niles it receives the [Dowagiac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dowagiac_River "Dowagiac River"). It divides [St. Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan "St. Joseph, Michigan") and [Benton Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benton_Harbor,_Michigan "Benton Harbor, Michigan"), receiving the [Paw Paw River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paw_Paw_River "Paw Paw River") from the north approximately 1 mile (1.6 km) from its mouth in St. Joseph on Lake Michigan.

There are 190 dams in the Saint Joseph River watershed, and 17 on the river mainstem.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Dams-6) Most of these dams block fish passage, although [fish ladders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_ladder "Fish ladder") constructed on the lower dams allow [salmonine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmonidae "Salmonidae") passage as far as the Twin Branch Dam in [Mishawaka, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mishawaka,_Indiana "Mishawaka, Indiana"). But, the fish ladders are not adequate for many native species, such as [sturgeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturgeon "Sturgeon"), and the dams tend to be built on the higher gradient portions of the river, which are the most critical river habitats for fish spawning.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Wesley-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/South-bend-st-joe-river.jpg/250px-South-bend-st-joe-river.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:South-bend-st-joe-river.jpg)

The Saint Joseph River flows through downtown South Bend, Indiana. The abrupt turn of the river gives the city its name.

**saakiiweesiipiiwi** (Outlet River, also historically spelt _Sakiwasipi_),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-8) as it was called by the Miami people, was inhabited for thousands of years by various indigenous tribes as it served an essential trade avenue in the Great Lakes region. The most recent indigenous inhabitants of the area were the [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_tribe "Miami tribe") and [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi") peoples.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-bogue-9) Two different [portages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portage "Portage") allowed nearly continuous travel by canoe among different watersheds of the region. The first major transfer point was at the headwaters in southwestern Michigan, where travelers could make a portage to the [Saint Joseph River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Maumee_River) "St. Joseph River (Maumee River)") of the Maumee River watershed, which drained into [Lake Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Erie "Lake Erie"). The second major transfer point was at South Bend, Indiana, where a short portage to the nearby [Kankakee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kankakee_River "Kankakee River") allowed access to the [Illinois River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_River "Illinois River") and subsequently to the Mississippi. Another major access point along river was at Niles, Michigan, where the [Old Sauk Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Sauk_Trail "Old Sauk Trail"), a major east-west Indian trail, crossed the river.

The indigenous trade and navigation networks in the area allowed for extensive trade and movement of people, which allowed early Europeans access to the area in 1675 when [Père Jacques Marquette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Marquette "Jacques Marquette") was guided up the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") via the Illinois River, then to the [Kankakee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kankakee_River "Kankakee River") and portaged to Sakiwasipi and then down to Lake Michigan. On November 1, 1679 [René Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Robert_Cavelier,_Sieur_de_La_Salle "René Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle") sailed southeast across Lake Michigan and built [Fort Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Miami_(Michigan) "Fort Miami (Michigan)") at the mouth of the river.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Howard-2) La Salle named the river _**La Rivière des Miamis**_ (River of the Miamis).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-McCafferty-1)

At the end of 1679, La Salle followed indigenous trade routes in the opposite direction of that taken by Marquette; heading up the St. Joseph River and portaging to the Kankakee River, getting as far west on the Illinois River as modern-day [Peoria, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peoria,_Illinois "Peoria, Illinois"), before returning to Fort Miami. After giving up on the return of his ship, _[Le Griffon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_Griffon "Le Griffon")_, in April 1680, he became the first European to walk the well traveled indigenous routes east across the [Lower Peninsula of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Peninsula_of_Michigan "Lower Peninsula of Michigan") back to the [Detroit River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_River "Detroit River") and Canada.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Howard-2)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-10) The French established [Fort St. Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_St._Joseph_(Niles) "Fort St. Joseph (Niles)") at the crossroads of [Old Sauk Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Sauk_Trail "Old Sauk Trail") and this well-established east–west trail in 1691.

The watershed was later used as [canoe route](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_canoe_routes "Canadian canoe routes") by early [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France")[fur trappers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_trade "Fur trade") in the [Illinois Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Country "Illinois Country"). [European American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_American "European American") settlement of the St. Joseph [river basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_basin "River basin") area began to increase in earnest after southwestern Michigan was surveyed in 1829.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-wesley-11) From the early 1830s until 1846, the river bore various commodities from upstream to a busy port at St. Joseph, where they were loaded onto lake boats for shipment to Chicago and elsewhere.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-bogue-9)

On April 11, 1893, a Lake Michigan _[seiche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seiche "Seiche")_ (a phenomenon similar to an ocean [tsunami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami "Tsunami")) pushed a wall of water, 3 to 5 feet (0.91 to 1.52 m) high, up the river at St. Joseph and Benton Harbor. This raised the level of the river by 4 to 5 feet (1.2 to 1.5 m). The cause of the seiche was unknown, but has been attributed to a sudden [squall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squall "Squall") or change in atmospheric pressure.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-12)

### South Bend Race Canals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: South Bend Race Canals")]

Factories located in [South Bend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bend "South Bend") because of access to the river and hydro-power created in the East and West Races.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-business_history-13) The water rights to what would become the East and West Races were claimed by [Alexis Coquillard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_Coquillard "Alexis Coquillard") and Lathrop Taylor in 1831, when the city of South Bend was founded.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-West_Race_St._Joe_River-14) Although the idea of digging a [mill race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mill_race "Mill race") (man-made canal) was put forth in 1835, a dam and the East and West Races were not constructed until 1843. The construction was done by the South Bend Manufacturing Company, incorporated in December 1842 for this very purpose. The South Bend Manufacturing Company thus became owner of the water power rights on the West Race canal, while Samuel L. Cottrell purchased the water rights along the East Race canal.

In 1867 the South Bend Hydraulic Company purchased the rights to the East Race canal for $100. In 1903 the ownership of stock, property rights, and property of the South Bend Manufacturing Company on the West Race canal passed to the [Oliver Chilled Plow Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Farm_Equipment_Company#Oliver_Chilled_Plow_Works "Oliver Farm Equipment Company").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-business_history-13) Over the next two years the Oliver Chilled Plow Works constructed a [hydro-electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydro-electric "Hydro-electric") power plant on the waterway to supply electricity for light, heat, and power to the Oliver Opera House, Oliver Hotel, South Bend factories, and other Oliver buildings.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Electricity-15)

Other sources of energy and changes in technology resulted in the canals no longer being used for industrial purposes. In the late 1940s the [Indiana and Michigan Electric Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Electric_Power#Indiana_Michigan_Power "American Electric Power") purchased the rights along the East Race canal. They began filling it in around 1954 for re-use for other purposes.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-business_history-13) In 1973 the Oliver Chilled Plow Works hydro-electric plant was demolished to make room for construction of the [Century Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_Center "Century Center"), which was completed in 1977.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-business_history-13) The West Race still exists as a canal North of Jefferson Boulevard and South of Colfax Avenue on the banks of Century Center, between Pier Park and Island Park.[_[original research?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No\_original\_research "Wikipedia:No original research")_]

In the early 1980s, the East Race canal was re-excavated. It was converted to a man-made whitewater [kayaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kayak "Kayak") course, now known as the East Race Waterway.

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/South-Bend-East-Race.jpg/250px-South-Bend-East-Race.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:South-Bend-East-Race.jpg)

East Race Waterway

In 1984, the abandoned East Race canal in South Bend, whose outlets were both at the river, was converted into the **East Race Waterway**, North America's first artificial [whitewater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitewater "Whitewater") waterway[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-erace-16) and the first of four in the United States.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-17) Locals first proposed in 1973 that the 19th-century waterway be reopened; construction began in August 1982 and the East Race reopened on June 29, 1984.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-18) Through the use of movable barriers and obstacles, the East Race can be configured to provide a whitewater course for recreational and competitive canoeing, kayaking and rafting. In 2021, the East Race was temporarily closed for construction. The City of [South Bend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bend "South Bend") is building a [hydroelectric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroelectric "Hydroelectric")[dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dam "Dam") on the waterway. The project was funded by the [University of Notre Dame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Notre_Dame "University of Notre Dame").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-19)

## Ecology and conservation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Ecology and conservation")]

Before European settlement, the watershed was dominated by [deciduous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deciduous "Deciduous") forests consisting of maple, ash, oak, elm, walnut, and beech species, along with pockets of white, red and jack pine species. There were also prairies up to several miles across, which were grazed by [elk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elk "Elk") (_Cervus canadensis_), [white-tailed deer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White-tailed_deer "White-tailed deer") (_Odocoileus virginianus_), [moose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moose "Moose") (_Alces alces_), and [bison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison "American bison") (_Bison bison_). By 1900 the virgin forests were mostly logged, and the prairies largely converted to agricultural use, as were many drained wetlands.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-WMP-5)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/08_30_2023_St_Joseph_River.png/250px-08_30_2023_St_Joseph_River.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:08_30_2023_St_Joseph_River.png)

Flora along the St. Joseph River bank plants at Union City, Michigan, in August 2023

Among the unique natural features that remain in the watershed are prairie [fens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fen "Fen"), coastal plain marshes, [bogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogs "Bogs"), floodplain forests, hardwood swamps, and moist hardwood forests. Rare plants include [prairie dropseed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sporobolus_heterolepis "Sporobolus heterolepis") (_Sporobolus heterolepis_), rosinweed, tall beak rush, and umbrella grass.

The wetlands and floodplain forests provide habitat to nearly half of all migratory birds in Indiana and Michigan and are a vital habitat for resident species as well, such as [wild turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_turkey "Wild turkey") (_Meleagris gallopavo_), [coyote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coyote "Coyote") (_Canis latrans_), fox, [beaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_beaver "North American beaver") (_Castor canadensis_), [mink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_mink "American mink") (_Neogale vison_), [Indiana bat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_bat "Indiana bat") (_Myotis sodalis_), [eastern box turtle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_box_turtle "Eastern box turtle") (_Terrapene carolina carolina_), and the rare [spotted turtle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotted_turtle "Spotted turtle") (_Clemmys guttata_) and [northern redbelly snake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_redbelly_snake "Northern redbelly snake") (_Storeria occipitomaculata occipitomaculata_), both protected by the state of Michigan. The lower Pigeon River is home to the federally endangered Indiana Bat.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-WMP-5)

In 1969, the [Michigan Department of Natural Resources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Department_of_Natural_Resources "Michigan Department of Natural Resources") began stocking the lower 23 miles (37 km) of the river for [steelhead trout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steelhead_trout "Steelhead trout") (_Oncorhynchus mykiss_), [Chinook salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinook_salmon "Chinook salmon") (_Oncorhynchus tshawytscha_) and [coho salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coho_salmon "Coho salmon") (_Oncorhynchus kisutch_). In 1975, Michigan constructed a fish ladder at the Berrien Springs Dam to enable the [salmonids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmonids "Salmonids") to run an additional 10 miles (16 km) upstream to the Buchanan Dam. In 1980 the Michigan Department of Natural Resources, [Indiana Department of Natural Resources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Department_of_Natural_Resources "Indiana Department of Natural Resources") and [United States Fish and Wildlife Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Fish_and_Wildlife_Service "United States Fish and Wildlife Service") signed the "St. Joseph River Interstate Cooperative Salmonid Management Plan", which led to construction of fish ladders at the Buchanan, Niles, South Bend and Mishawaka dams. By 1992 the [salmonid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmonid "Salmonid") runs were extended to the Twin Branch Dam in Indiana, a distance of 63 miles (101 km) from Lake Michigan. This enabled the trout and salmon to spawn in coldwater tributaries such as [McCoy Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Creek_(Michigan) "McCoy Creek (Michigan)").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-WMP-5)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-MDNR-20)

Although completion of fish ladders on the lowest five mainstem dams in 1992 allowed [salmonine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmonidae "Salmonidae") passage as far as Twin Branch Dam in [Mishawaka, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mishawaka,_Indiana "Mishawaka, Indiana"), 94% of the fish that pass are salmon and trout, as the ladders were not designed to permit passage of migrating native fish. Historically, the migrating native species included [lake sturgeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_sturgeon "Lake sturgeon") (_Acipenser fulvescens_), bass (smallmouth and largemouth), [redhorse (silver, golden, shorthead, river, and greater)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redhorse "Redhorse") (_Moxostoma ssp._), [walleye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walleye "Walleye") (_Sander vitreus_), [lake trout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_trout "Lake trout") (_Salvelinus namaycush_), [lake whitefish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_whitefish "Lake whitefish") (_Coregonus clupeaformis_), [northern pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_pike "Northern pike") (_Esox lucius_) and [American pickerel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_pickerel "American pickerel") (_E. americanus vermiculatus_). Every spring the [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi") and early settlers used spears, seines and dip nets to catch their annual supply of fish. The abundance of lake sturgeon made the area around [Niles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niles,_Michigan "Niles, Michigan") famous in the mid-to late-1800s. Fish up to 12 feet (3.7 m) long and 300 pounds (140 kg) were taken by anglers, and their [roe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe "Roe") was exported to Russia as caviar. Sturgeon used to migrate as far as [Hillsdale County, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsdale_County,_Michigan "Hillsdale County, Michigan"), and [Sturgeon Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturgeon_Lake_(Michigan)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sturgeon Lake (Michigan) (page does not exist)") near [Colon, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colon,_Michigan "Colon, Michigan"), still bears the name of this mighty fish.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-21) Now the spawning sturgeon rarely reach Niles, as they are impeded by the dam at [Berrien Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_Springs,_Michigan "Berrien Springs, Michigan"), reducing the length of the river used by them for spawning by 155 miles (249 km). Historically, ninety-seven species of fish were native to the Saint Joseph River Basin.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Wesley-7)

In 1994, the Friends of the Saint Joe River (FotSJR), a non-profit conservation organization, was founded by [Athens, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens,_Michigan "Athens, Michigan"), residents Al and Margaret Smith, to organize the river communities to clean and restore the river. In 2002 FotSJR developed the St. Joseph River Watershed Management Plan, with grant support from the [Michigan Department of Environmental Quality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Department_of_Environmental_Quality "Michigan Department of Environmental Quality"). The river delivers significant pollutants to Lake Michigan - including sewage overflows from riverside communities, sediments and toxic substances such as mercury and [polychlorinated biphenyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polychlorinated_biphenyl "Polychlorinated biphenyl") (PCB).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-WMP-5) When the plan was developed, the river carried the greatest portion of [atrazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atrazine "Atrazine") into Lake Michigan. It is an agricultural herbicide associated with cancer even at low levels and is a very common contaminant of drinking water.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-22)

## Recreation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Recreation")]

The Saint Joseph River is a trout and salmon sport fishery, encompassing 47 miles (76 km) of river in Michigan and 16 miles (26 km) in Indiana. The economic benefits to local Michigan and Indiana communities are estimated at several million dollars annually.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-MDNR-20)

Canoeists can travel the entire length of the main stem, if they are prepared to portage. Many of the larger tributaries offer opportunities for paddling, hiking, hunting, and fishing.

The **Saint Joseph River** (known locally as the **Saint Joe**) is a 210-mile-long (340 km)[river](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River "River") that flows in a generally westerly direction through [southern Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Michigan "Southern Michigan") and [northern Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Indiana "Northern Indiana"), United States, before emptying into [Lake Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Michigan "Lake Michigan"). The Saint Joseph River [drainage basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") covers 4,685 square miles (12,130 km 2), and is the third largest watershed draining to Lake Michigan. The land within its bounds is primarily used for [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture"). The river and its tributaries provide a variety of [paddling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddling "Paddling") and fishing environments. Historically, the river served as an important [canoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canoe "Canoe") transportation route for various [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") tribes, and for [French Canadian Voyageurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyageurs "Voyageurs").

## Description of the watershed

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description of the watershed")]

The Saint Joseph River watershed drains 4,685 square miles (12,130 km 2) from 15 counties: [Berrien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_County,_Michigan "Berrien County, Michigan"), [Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branch_County,_Michigan "Branch County, Michigan"), [Calhoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calhoun_County,_Michigan "Calhoun County, Michigan"), [Cass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_Michigan "Cass County, Michigan"), [Hillsdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsdale_County,_Michigan "Hillsdale County, Michigan"), [Kalamazoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalamazoo_County,_Michigan "Kalamazoo County, Michigan"), [Saint Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_County,_Michigan "St. Joseph County, Michigan") and [Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Buren_County,_Michigan "Van Buren County, Michigan") in Michigan and [DeKalb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeKalb_County,_Indiana "DeKalb County, Indiana"), [Elkhart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elkhart_County,_Indiana "Elkhart County, Indiana"), [Kosciusko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosciusko_County,_Indiana "Kosciusko County, Indiana"), [LaGrange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaGrange_County,_Indiana "LaGrange County, Indiana"), [Noble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_County,_Indiana "Noble County, Indiana"), [Saint Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_County,_Indiana "St. Joseph County, Indiana") and [Steuben](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steuben_County,_Indiana "Steuben County, Indiana") in Indiana. The watershed includes 3,742 river miles (6,022 km) and flows through and near the Kalamazoo-Portage, Elkhart-Goshen, Mishawaka-South Bend, and Saint Joseph/Benton Harbor metropolitan areas.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-WMP-5) The St. Joseph River main stem is 206 miles (332 km) long, rising in southern Michigan in [Hillsdale County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsdale_County,_Michigan "Hillsdale County, Michigan") flowing from [Baw Beese Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baw_Beese_Lake "Baw Beese Lake"), within 5 miles (8 km) of the headwaters of the other Saint Joseph River of the eastward-flowing [Maumee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maumee_River "Maumee River") watershed. Baw Beese Lake was historically named for the [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi") Chief [Baw Beese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baw_Beese "Baw Beese").

The river follows a zigzag route generally westward across southern Michigan, dipping into northern Indiana. From its headwaters, it flows initially northwest past [Hillsdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsdale,_Michigan "Hillsdale, Michigan") into southeastern [Calhoun County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calhoun_County,_Michigan "Calhoun County, Michigan"), then turns abruptly southwest to flow past [Tekonsha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekonsha,_Michigan "Tekonsha, Michigan"), [Union City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_City,_Michigan "Union City, Michigan"), [Sherwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherwood,_Michigan "Sherwood, Michigan"), and [Mendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendon,_Michigan "Mendon, Michigan"). At [Three Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Rivers,_Michigan "Three Rivers, Michigan") it is joined from the north by the [Rocky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_River_(Michigan) "Rocky River (Michigan)") and [Portage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portage_River_(St._Joseph_County) "Portage River (St. Joseph County)") rivers, and by the [Prairie River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prairie_River_(Michigan) "Prairie River (Michigan)") from the east, after making an abrupt turn south. At [Constantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine,_Michigan "Constantine, Michigan") it receives the [Fawn River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fawn_River_(Michigan) "Fawn River (Michigan)") from the east. Next, after returning to a southwest course, it receives the [Pigeon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeon_River_(St._Joseph_River)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pigeon River (St. Joseph River) (page does not exist)") from the east, near the Michigan–[Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana") state line. In northern Indiana, the river flows west-southwest through [Elkhart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elkhart,_Indiana "Elkhart, Indiana"), [Mishawaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mishawaka "Mishawaka"), and South Bend, where it turns abruptly north to re-enter southwestern Michigan in southeastern [Berrien County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_County,_Michigan "Berrien County, Michigan"). In southwestern Michigan, it follows a wide [meandering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meander "Meander") route generally northwest through [Niles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niles,_Michigan "Niles, Michigan") and past [Berrien Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_Springs,_Michigan "Berrien Springs, Michigan"). Just North of Niles it receives the [Dowagiac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dowagiac_River "Dowagiac River"). It divides [St. Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan "St. Joseph, Michigan") and [Benton Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benton_Harbor,_Michigan "Benton Harbor, Michigan"), receiving the [Paw Paw River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paw_Paw_River "Paw Paw River") from the north approximately 1 mile (1.6 km) from its mouth in St. Joseph on Lake Michigan.

There are 190 dams in the Saint Joseph River watershed, and 17 on the river mainstem.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Dams-6) Most of these dams block fish passage, although [fish ladders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_ladder "Fish ladder") constructed on the lower dams allow [salmonine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmonidae "Salmonidae") passage as far as the Twin Branch Dam in [Mishawaka, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mishawaka,_Indiana "Mishawaka, Indiana"). But, the fish ladders are not adequate for many native species, such as [sturgeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturgeon "Sturgeon"), and the dams tend to be built on the higher gradient portions of the river, which are the most critical river habitats for fish spawning.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Wesley-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/South-bend-st-joe-river.jpg/250px-South-bend-st-joe-river.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:South-bend-st-joe-river.jpg)

The Saint Joseph River flows through downtown South Bend, Indiana. The abrupt turn of the river gives the city its name.

**saakiiweesiipiiwi** (Outlet River, also historically spelt _Sakiwasipi_),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-8) as it was called by the Miami people, was inhabited for thousands of years by various indigenous tribes as it served an essential trade avenue in the Great Lakes region. The most recent indigenous inhabitants of the area were the [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_tribe "Miami tribe") and [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi") peoples.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-bogue-9) Two different [portages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portage "Portage") allowed nearly continuous travel by canoe among different watersheds of the region. The first major transfer point was at the headwaters in southwestern Michigan, where travelers could make a portage to the [Saint Joseph River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Maumee_River) "St. Joseph River (Maumee River)") of the Maumee River watershed, which drained into [Lake Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Erie "Lake Erie"). The second major transfer point was at South Bend, Indiana, where a short portage to the nearby [Kankakee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kankakee_River "Kankakee River") allowed access to the [Illinois River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_River "Illinois River") and subsequently to the Mississippi. Another major access point along river was at Niles, Michigan, where the [Old Sauk Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Sauk_Trail "Old Sauk Trail"), a major east-west Indian trail, crossed the river.

The indigenous trade and navigation networks in the area allowed for extensive trade and movement of people, which allowed early Europeans access to the area in 1675 when [Père Jacques Marquette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Marquette "Jacques Marquette") was guided up the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") via the Illinois River, then to the [Kankakee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kankakee_River "Kankakee River") and portaged to Sakiwasipi and then down to Lake Michigan. On November 1, 1679 [René Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Robert_Cavelier,_Sieur_de_La_Salle "René Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle") sailed southeast across Lake Michigan and built [Fort Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Miami_(Michigan) "Fort Miami (Michigan)") at the mouth of the river.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Howard-2) La Salle named the river _**La Rivière des Miamis**_ (River of the Miamis).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-McCafferty-1)

At the end of 1679, La Salle followed indigenous trade routes in the opposite direction of that taken by Marquette; heading up the St. Joseph River and portaging to the Kankakee River, getting as far west on the Illinois River as modern-day [Peoria, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peoria,_Illinois "Peoria, Illinois"), before returning to Fort Miami. After giving up on the return of his ship, _[Le Griffon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_Griffon "Le Griffon")_, in April 1680, he became the first European to walk the well traveled indigenous routes east across the [Lower Peninsula of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Peninsula_of_Michigan "Lower Peninsula of Michigan") back to the [Detroit River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_River "Detroit River") and Canada.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Howard-2)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-10) The French established [Fort St. Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_St._Joseph_(Niles) "Fort St. Joseph (Niles)") at the crossroads of [Old Sauk Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Sauk_Trail "Old Sauk Trail") and this well-established east–west trail in 1691.

The watershed was later used as [canoe route](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_canoe_routes "Canadian canoe routes") by early [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France")[fur trappers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_trade "Fur trade") in the [Illinois Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Country "Illinois Country"). [European American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_American "European American") settlement of the St. Joseph [river basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_basin "River basin") area began to increase in earnest after southwestern Michigan was surveyed in 1829.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-wesley-11) From the early 1830s until 1846, the river bore various commodities from upstream to a busy port at St. Joseph, where they were loaded onto lake boats for shipment to Chicago and elsewhere.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-bogue-9)

On April 11, 1893, a Lake Michigan _[seiche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seiche "Seiche")_ (a phenomenon similar to an ocean [tsunami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami "Tsunami")) pushed a wall of water, 3 to 5 feet (0.91 to 1.52 m) high, up the river at St. Joseph and Benton Harbor. This raised the level of the river by 4 to 5 feet (1.2 to 1.5 m). The cause of the seiche was unknown, but has been attributed to a sudden [squall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squall "Squall") or change in atmospheric pressure.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-12)

### South Bend Race Canals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: South Bend Race Canals")]

Factories located in [South Bend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bend "South Bend") because of access to the river and hydro-power created in the East and West Races.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-business_history-13) The water rights to what would become the East and West Races were claimed by [Alexis Coquillard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_Coquillard "Alexis Coquillard") and Lathrop Taylor in 1831, when the city of South Bend was founded.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-West_Race_St._Joe_River-14) Although the idea of digging a [mill race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mill_race "Mill race") (man-made canal) was put forth in 1835, a dam and the East and West Races were not constructed until 1843. The construction was done by the South Bend Manufacturing Company, incorporated in December 1842 for this very purpose. The South Bend Manufacturing Company thus became owner of the water power rights on the West Race canal, while Samuel L. Cottrell purchased the water rights along the East Race canal.

In 1867 the South Bend Hydraulic Company purchased the rights to the East Race canal for $100. In 1903 the ownership of stock, property rights, and property of the South Bend Manufacturing Company on the West Race canal passed to the [Oliver Chilled Plow Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Farm_Equipment_Company#Oliver_Chilled_Plow_Works "Oliver Farm Equipment Company").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-business_history-13) Over the next two years the Oliver Chilled Plow Works constructed a [hydro-electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydro-electric "Hydro-electric") power plant on the waterway to supply electricity for light, heat, and power to the Oliver Opera House, Oliver Hotel, South Bend factories, and other Oliver buildings.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Electricity-15)

Other sources of energy and changes in technology resulted in the canals no longer being used for industrial purposes. In the late 1940s the [Indiana and Michigan Electric Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Electric_Power#Indiana_Michigan_Power "American Electric Power") purchased the rights along the East Race canal. They began filling it in around 1954 for re-use for other purposes.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-business_history-13) In 1973 the Oliver Chilled Plow Works hydro-electric plant was demolished to make room for construction of the [Century Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_Center "Century Center"), which was completed in 1977.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-business_history-13) The West Race still exists as a canal North of Jefferson Boulevard and South of Colfax Avenue on the banks of Century Center, between Pier Park and Island Park.[_[original research?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No\_original\_research "Wikipedia:No original research")_]

In the early 1980s, the East Race canal was re-excavated. It was converted to a man-made whitewater [kayaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kayak "Kayak") course, now known as the East Race Waterway.

#### East Race Waterway

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: East Race Waterway")]

[41°40′34″N 86°14′42″W / 41.676°N 86.245°W / 41.676; -86.245](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&params=41.676_N_86.245_W_)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/South-Bend-East-Race.jpg/250px-South-Bend-East-Race.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:South-Bend-East-Race.jpg)

East Race Waterway

In 1984, the abandoned East Race canal in South Bend, whose outlets were both at the river, was converted into the **East Race Waterway**, North America's first artificial [whitewater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitewater "Whitewater") waterway[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-erace-16) and the first of four in the United States.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-17) Locals first proposed in 1973 that the 19th-century waterway be reopened; construction began in August 1982 and the East Race reopened on June 29, 1984.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-18) Through the use of movable barriers and obstacles, the East Race can be configured to provide a whitewater course for recreational and competitive canoeing, kayaking and rafting. In 2021, the East Race was temporarily closed for construction. The City of [South Bend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bend "South Bend") is building a [hydroelectric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroelectric "Hydroelectric")[dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dam "Dam") on the waterway. The project was funded by the [University of Notre Dame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Notre_Dame "University of Notre Dame").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-19)

## Ecology and conservation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Ecology and conservation")]

Before European settlement, the watershed was dominated by [deciduous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deciduous "Deciduous") forests consisting of maple, ash, oak, elm, walnut, and beech species, along with pockets of white, red and jack pine species. There were also prairies up to several miles across, which were grazed by [elk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elk "Elk") (_Cervus canadensis_), [white-tailed deer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White-tailed_deer "White-tailed deer") (_Odocoileus virginianus_), [moose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moose "Moose") (_Alces alces_), and [bison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison "American bison") (_Bison bison_). By 1900 the virgin forests were mostly logged, and the prairies largely converted to agricultural use, as were many drained wetlands.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-WMP-5)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/08_30_2023_St_Joseph_River.png/250px-08_30_2023_St_Joseph_River.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:08_30_2023_St_Joseph_River.png)

Flora along the St. Joseph River bank plants at Union City, Michigan, in August 2023

Among the unique natural features that remain in the watershed are prairie [fens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fen "Fen"), coastal plain marshes, [bogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogs "Bogs"), floodplain forests, hardwood swamps, and moist hardwood forests. Rare plants include [prairie dropseed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sporobolus_heterolepis "Sporobolus heterolepis") (_Sporobolus heterolepis_), rosinweed, tall beak rush, and umbrella grass.

The wetlands and floodplain forests provide habitat to nearly half of all migratory birds in Indiana and Michigan and are a vital habitat for resident species as well, such as [wild turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_turkey "Wild turkey") (_Meleagris gallopavo_), [coyote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coyote "Coyote") (_Canis latrans_), fox, [beaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_beaver "North American beaver") (_Castor canadensis_), [mink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_mink "American mink") (_Neogale vison_), [Indiana bat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_bat "Indiana bat") (_Myotis sodalis_), [eastern box turtle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_box_turtle "Eastern box turtle") (_Terrapene carolina carolina_), and the rare [spotted turtle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotted_turtle "Spotted turtle") (_Clemmys guttata_) and [northern redbelly snake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_redbelly_snake "Northern redbelly snake") (_Storeria occipitomaculata occipitomaculata_), both protected by the state of Michigan. The lower Pigeon River is home to the federally endangered Indiana Bat.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-WMP-5)

In 1969, the [Michigan Department of Natural Resources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Department_of_Natural_Resources "Michigan Department of Natural Resources") began stocking the lower 23 miles (37 km) of the river for [steelhead trout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steelhead_trout "Steelhead trout") (_Oncorhynchus mykiss_), [Chinook salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinook_salmon "Chinook salmon") (_Oncorhynchus tshawytscha_) and [coho salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coho_salmon "Coho salmon") (_Oncorhynchus kisutch_). In 1975, Michigan constructed a fish ladder at the Berrien Springs Dam to enable the [salmonids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmonids "Salmonids") to run an additional 10 miles (16 km) upstream to the Buchanan Dam. In 1980 the Michigan Department of Natural Resources, [Indiana Department of Natural Resources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Department_of_Natural_Resources "Indiana Department of Natural Resources") and [United States Fish and Wildlife Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Fish_and_Wildlife_Service "United States Fish and Wildlife Service") signed the "St. Joseph River Interstate Cooperative Salmonid Management Plan", which led to construction of fish ladders at the Buchanan, Niles, South Bend and Mishawaka dams. By 1992 the [salmonid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmonid "Salmonid") runs were extended to the Twin Branch Dam in Indiana, a distance of 63 miles (101 km) from Lake Michigan. This enabled the trout and salmon to spawn in coldwater tributaries such as [McCoy Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Creek_(Michigan) "McCoy Creek (Michigan)").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-WMP-5)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-MDNR-20)

Although completion of fish ladders on the lowest five mainstem dams in 1992 allowed [salmonine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmonidae "Salmonidae") passage as far as Twin Branch Dam in [Mishawaka, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mishawaka,_Indiana "Mishawaka, Indiana"), 94% of the fish that pass are salmon and trout, as the ladders were not designed to permit passage of migrating native fish. Historically, the migrating native species included [lake sturgeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_sturgeon "Lake sturgeon") (_Acipenser fulvescens_), bass (smallmouth and largemouth), [redhorse (silver, golden, shorthead, river, and greater)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redhorse "Redhorse") (_Moxostoma ssp._), [walleye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walleye "Walleye") (_Sander vitreus_), [lake trout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_trout "Lake trout") (_Salvelinus namaycush_), [lake whitefish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_whitefish "Lake whitefish") (_Coregonus clupeaformis_), [northern pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_pike "Northern pike") (_Esox lucius_) and [American pickerel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_pickerel "American pickerel") (_E. americanus vermiculatus_). Every spring the [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi") and early settlers used spears, seines and dip nets to catch their annual supply of fish. The abundance of lake sturgeon made the area around [Niles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niles,_Michigan "Niles, Michigan") famous in the mid-to late-1800s. Fish up to 12 feet (3.7 m) long and 300 pounds (140 kg) were taken by anglers, and their [roe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe "Roe") was exported to Russia as caviar. Sturgeon used to migrate as far as [Hillsdale County, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsdale_County,_Michigan "Hillsdale County, Michigan"), and [Sturgeon Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturgeon_Lake_(Michigan)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sturgeon Lake (Michigan) (page does not exist)") near [Colon, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colon,_Michigan "Colon, Michigan"), still bears the name of this mighty fish.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-21) Now the spawning sturgeon rarely reach Niles, as they are impeded by the dam at [Berrien Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_Springs,_Michigan "Berrien Springs, Michigan"), reducing the length of the river used by them for spawning by 155 miles (249 km). Historically, ninety-seven species of fish were native to the Saint Joseph River Basin.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-Wesley-7)

In 1994, the Friends of the Saint Joe River (FotSJR), a non-profit conservation organization, was founded by [Athens, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens,_Michigan "Athens, Michigan"), residents Al and Margaret Smith, to organize the river communities to clean and restore the river. In 2002 FotSJR developed the St. Joseph River Watershed Management Plan, with grant support from the [Michigan Department of Environmental Quality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Department_of_Environmental_Quality "Michigan Department of Environmental Quality"). The river delivers significant pollutants to Lake Michigan - including sewage overflows from riverside communities, sediments and toxic substances such as mercury and [polychlorinated biphenyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polychlorinated_biphenyl "Polychlorinated biphenyl") (PCB).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-WMP-5) When the plan was developed, the river carried the greatest portion of [atrazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atrazine "Atrazine") into Lake Michigan. It is an agricultural herbicide associated with cancer even at low levels and is a very common contaminant of drinking water.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-22)

## Recreation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Recreation")]

The Saint Joseph River is a trout and salmon sport fishery, encompassing 47 miles (76 km) of river in Michigan and 16 miles (26 km) in Indiana. The economic benefits to local Michigan and Indiana communities are estimated at several million dollars annually.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan)#cite_note-MDNR-20)

Canoeists can travel the entire length of the main stem, if they are prepared to portage. Many of the larger tributaries offer opportunities for paddling, hiking, hunting, and fishing.

**Saint Joseph**, colloquially known as **Saint Joe**, is a city in and the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Berrien County, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_County,_Michigan "Berrien County, Michigan"). It was incorporated as a village in 1834 and as a city in 1891.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoolidge1906[httpsarchiveorgdetailsbad08550001001umichedu_25]-4) As of the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_2020_Census "United States 2020 Census"), the city population was 7,856.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-2020_census-5) It lies on the shore of [Lake Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Michigan "Lake Michigan"), at the mouth of the [St. Joseph River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan) "St. Joseph River (Lake Michigan)"), about 90 miles (140 km) east-northeast of Chicago.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-GR6-6) The city and adjacent [Benton Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benton_Harbor,_Michigan "Benton Harbor, Michigan") are known as the "Twin Cities".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Michigan&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The mouth of the Saint Joseph River at present day Saint Joseph was an important point of Miami and Potawatomi travel and commerce, as it lay along a key water route between the [Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes "Great Lakes") and the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"). Both the [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_tribe "Miami tribe") and [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi") used this route and would use the area as a camp.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-8) The St. Joseph River also allowed for connection with the [Sauk Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauk_Trail "Sauk Trail"), which was the major land trail through Michigan. In 1669, the mouth of the river was seen by European explorers. French explorer [René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9-Robert_Cavelier,_Sieur_de_La_Salle "René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle"), built [Fort Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Miami_(Michigan) "Fort Miami (Michigan)") on the bluff overlooking Lake Michigan.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-9) In 1678, he waited for the ship _[Le Griffon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_Griffon "Le Griffon")_, which never returned. Once the ship was deemed lost, La Salle and his men made the first land crossing of the lower peninsula by Europeans.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEccles1997[httpsbooksgooglecombooksid8N4ckSmAiL0CpgPA134_134]-10)

The next permanent white settler in Saint Joseph was William Burnett, who around 1780 started a [trading post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_post "Trading post") at the mouth of the Saint Joseph River.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoolidge1906[httpsbooksgooglecombooksid3G0Qo9lf4nsCpage19_19]-11) The post traded food, furs and goods with places including Detroit, Mackinac and Chicago.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-hist-12) In 1829, [Calvin Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Britain "Calvin Britain"), who had come from [Jefferson County, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_County,_New_York "Jefferson County, New York"), and had taught at the [Carey Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carey_Mission "Carey Mission") at [Niles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niles,_Michigan "Niles, Michigan") for two years, came to the site of Saint Joseph.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFuller1916[httpsarchiveorgdetailseconomicsocialbe01fullpage276_266]-13) Shortly thereafter, he laid out the plat of the village, then known as Newburyport, named after [a coastal city in Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newburyport,_Massachusetts "Newburyport, Massachusetts"). Britain was influential in attracting other settlers to the area. Lots sold rapidly and the village flourished.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFuller1916[httpsarchiveorgdetailseconomicsocialbe01fullpage275_275%E2%80%9376.]-14)

The Saint Joseph river mouth was straightened through a channel and piers were added later. The first [lighthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse "Lighthouse") in Saint Joseph contends with Chicago's original lighthouse as the first to be built on Lake Michigan. Newburyport changed its name to St. Joseph when it was incorporated on March 7, 1834.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-hist-12) The city was incorporated June 5, 1891.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] It was reported in 2026 that the same year, a merger had been attempted between St. Joseph and Benton Harbor.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-15)

The first water route across Lake Michigan between Saint Joseph and Chicago began as a mail route in 1825, but service was sporadic until 1842 when Samuel and Eber Ward began a permanent service. That lasted eleven years. Before the rise of large ship companies on Lake Michigan, service was done primarily by owner-operated boats. With the rise in shipping in Benton Harbor and the rise in tourism in Saint Joseph, permanent and larger operations began operating out of the ports.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHilton2002-16)

The Coast Guard still maintains a station on this site.[[A]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-18) In 1876 the [United States Lifesaving Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Lifesaving_Service "United States Lifesaving Service") built a Lifesaving Station at Saint Joseph, appointing [Joseph Napier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Napier_(USCG) "Joseph Napier (USCG)") as the first stationkeeper.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-UscgBioJosephNapier-17)

After a bitterly fought political contest, Saint Joseph was named the seat of Berrien County in 1894, when [Berrien Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_Springs,_Michigan "Berrien Springs, Michigan") relinquished that status. The three largest towns in the county, [Benton Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benton_Harbor "Benton Harbor"), Saint Joseph, and [Niles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niles,_Michigan "Niles, Michigan"), each wanted to be the county seat, but none had a majority vote. Once St. Joseph and Benton Harbor voters combined their votes, St. Joseph had enough to win.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFedynsky2010[httpsbooksgooglecombooksidogrel7yYnvQCpgPA25_25]-19)

On October 11, 1898, [Augustus Moore Herring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Moore_Herring "Augustus Moore Herring") took one of his [gliders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glider_aircraft "Glider aircraft"), fitted with a motor, to [Silver Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Beach_Amusement_Park "Silver Beach Amusement Park") in Saint Joseph. Herring's machine lifted ever so slightly off the ground and actually flew for seven seconds. Eleven days later, the inventor made another flight of ten seconds. While Herring had a powered heavier-than-air craft, he did not have a way to control it. It was left to the [Wright brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_brothers "Wright brothers") to perfect controlled flight five years later, and give themselves and [Kitty Hawk, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitty_Hawk,_North_Carolina "Kitty Hawk, North Carolina"), a place in history that might have ended up belonging to Herring and Saint Joseph.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-20)

### Transportation history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Michigan&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Transportation history")]

Two major shipping companies operated between Saint Joseph and Chicago during the last half of the 19th century, the Goodrich Transportation Company and the local firm of Graham and Morton. They dominated the traffic at St. Joseph for more than 100 years, although other smaller companies did operate during this time.

Starting in 1874, Henry Graham and J. Stanley Morton began operating a steam line out of St. Joseph. Their collaboration would become the Graham and Morton Transportation Company.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-21) Through vigorous competition, they won the war to become the major carrier out of Saint Joseph. Goodrich stopped service to the Twin Cities in 1880. The company grew quickly and over the fifty plus years of its existence became the second largest line on Lake Michigan, behind only Goodrich.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHilton2002-16)

In 1924, as graded roads began to line the Lake Michigan shoreline, G & M was forced to merge into Goodrich. Like most other ports along Lake Michigan, Saint Joseph saw a large drop in traffic during the early years of the twentieth century, which was exacerbated further by the Great Depression. The route between Chicago and St. Joseph survived until the 1950s.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHilton2002-16)

On January 29, 1870, the [Chicago and Michigan Lake Shore Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_and_Michigan_Lake_Shore_Railroad "Chicago and Michigan Lake Shore Railroad") extended a rail line from [New Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Buffalo,_Michigan "New Buffalo, Michigan") to St. Joseph. This railroad connected Saint Joseph to [Grand Rapids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Rapids,_Michigan "Grand Rapids, Michigan"), [Muskegon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muskegon,_Michigan "Muskegon, Michigan"), Detroit and Chicago. (Prior to this, the only connection Saint Joseph had to these other cities was by water.) The line was reorganized as the [Chicago and West Michigan Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_and_West_Michigan_Railway "Chicago and West Michigan Railway") and then was incorporated into the [Pere Marquette Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pere_Marquette_Railroad "Pere Marquette Railroad"). Nowadays it is recognized as the CSX Grand Rapids Subdivision which runs from Chicago, IL to Grand Rapids, MI along the former Pere Marquette Railroad. Passenger Rail Service is provided by Amtrak's "Pere Marquette" service running from Chicago, IL to Grand Rapids, MI, with stops in St. Joseph, Bangor, Holland, and Grand Rapids. Service is offered with one daily round trip.

### Business and industry history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Michigan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Business and industry history")]

In 1892, Truscott Boat Manufacturing Co moved to Saint Joseph from Grand Rapids. In the early 20th Century, the company was the largest employer in St. Joseph with 700 employees and built 600 wooden boats per year. The company built boats for the government in World War I, struggled during the Depression, was sold in 1940, revived during World War II to build ships for the Navy and went bankrupt in 1948.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-22)

In 1911, [Louis, Emory, and Frederick Upton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_and_Louis_Upton "Frederick and Louis Upton") began a business that produced household [washing machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washing_machine "Washing machine"). The business soon became a boom and has continued to grow to this day. In 1929, Upton Machine Company merged with Nineteen Hundred Corp., taking the latter name. The company began marketing a line of appliances known as the "Whirlpool" brand in 1948. Within the next decade, Nineteen Hundred changed its name to Whirlpool. Today, [Whirlpool Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whirlpool_Corporation "Whirlpool Corporation") is the largest manufacturer of major home appliances and maintains a large presence in Benton Harbor and nearby Saint Joseph. Whirlpool has its world headquarters in Benton Harbor.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-23)

In 1891 the [Silver Beach Amusement Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Beach_Amusement_Park "Silver Beach Amusement Park") was opened on land between the lake and mouth of the river in Saint Joseph. Logan Drake and Louis Wallace bought the land from the [Pere Marquette Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pere_Marquette_Railroad "Pere Marquette Railroad") and added cottages to lure tourists to the lake front. As the park aged and grew in popularity, the pair added many attractions, including concessions, games, pool, a boardwalk and different rides. The first [roller coaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roller_coaster "Roller coaster") was built in 1904 and was called the Chase Through the Clouds, which was replaced by the Velvet roller coaster (renamed the Comet). Among the most popular attractions were the [carousel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carousel "Carousel") and the Shadowland Ballroom, built in 1927. During the 1960s and 1970s, the buildings decayed and the crowds decreased. Finally, crime in the park led police to shut it down in 1970.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-24)

The [American Society of Agricultural and Biological Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Society_of_Agricultural_and_Biological_Engineers "American Society of Agricultural and Biological Engineers") is based in St. Joseph.

City government is organized as a [council-manager government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council-manager_government "Council-manager government"). There is a city commission with five members, who are elected at large. City elections are held in November of even-numbered years; at each election, three commission seats become open. The two candidates receiving the greatest number of votes receive four-year terms, while the candidate receiving the third-greatest number of votes receives a two-year term. At the first meeting following each election, the commission selects from its own number a mayor and mayor pro tem for the following two years. The city commission is a part-time body, typically meeting twice each month to act as a legislative body and set general policies. Day-to-day operations are delegated to a contracted [city manager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_manager "City manager").

Major city facilities include the City Hall and Police Station at 700 Broad Street; the Department of Public Works at 1160 Broad Street; the Fire Department at 915 Broad Street; the Maud Preston Palenske Public Library at 500 Market Street; the John and Dede Howard Ice Arena at 2414 Willa Drive; the Water Treatment Plant at 1701 Lions Park Drive; and Riverview Cemetery at 2525 Niles Road.

The city Water Treatment Plant provides drinking water to the communities of the Lake Michigan Shoreline Water and Sewage Treatment Authority, which serves [Lincoln Charter Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Charter_Township,_Michigan "Lincoln Charter Township, Michigan"), [Royalton Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royalton_Township,_Michigan "Royalton Township, Michigan"), [Saint Joseph Charter Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_Charter_Township,_Michigan "St. Joseph Charter Township, Michigan"), and the villages of [Shoreham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoreham,_Michigan "Shoreham, Michigan") and [Stevensville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevensville,_Michigan "Stevensville, Michigan"). Wastewater treatment is provided through the Joint Wastewater Treatment Plant, which is jointly owned by the cities of St. Joseph and Benton Harbor, and which also serves the LMSWSTA communities, [Benton Charter Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benton_Charter_Township,_Michigan "Benton Charter Township, Michigan") and portions of [Sodus Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodus_Township,_Michigan "Sodus Township, Michigan").

## Culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Michigan&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Culture")]

Saint Joseph is cohost of the annual Blossomtime Festival[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-35) with Benton Harbor.

The Krasl Art Fair on the Bluff[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-36) is held in Lake Bluff Park every year on the weekend after the July 4 weekend.

The Concours d'Elegance of Southwest Michigan is held annually on the second Saturday in August. The inaugural show was held in 2005. An invitational fine car show, 75 vintage car owners are asked to show vehicles in St. Joseph's downtown Lake Bluff Park.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-37)

### Venetian Festival

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Michigan&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Venetian Festival")]

From 1979 to 2011, St. Joseph was the site of the Venetian Festival, which comprised three traditions: the Blessing of the River, the Lighted Boat Parade, and a Classic Boat Parade. The festival's name was a nod to similarities between Saint Joseph and [Venice, Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice,_Italy "Venice, Italy").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-venetian.org-38)

In 1987, [USS _Oliver Hazard Perry_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Oliver_Hazard_Perry "USS Oliver Hazard Perry") came to port, and its commander let festival-goers take a free tour. This initiated a tradition whereby [US Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Navy "US Navy")[ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ships "Ships") regularly came to the festival. Music also contributed to the festival's success, and was offered at three locations: the [Bluff](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/bluff#Etymology_2 "wikt:bluff"), [Shadowland Pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadowland_Pavilion?action=edit&redlink=1 "Shadowland Pavilion (page does not exist)"), and the Main Stage. Many local musicians played at the Bluff and the Pavilion, while the Main Stage hosted such well-known bands as the [Beach Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beach_Boys "Beach Boys"), [Cheap Trick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheap_Trick "Cheap Trick"), [Gin Blossoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gin_Blossoms "Gin Blossoms"), [Little Big Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Big_Town "Little Big Town"), and [Jason Michael Carroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Michael_Carroll "Jason Michael Carroll").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In a study done by Michigan State University in 1998, approximately 63,000 people attended the 1997 Venetian Festival and the festival generated around $1.7 million in revenue to the local economy.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-39)

Competitions also took place along [Silver Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Beach_Amusement_Park "Silver Beach Amusement Park") and the [Saint Joseph River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_River_(Lake_Michigan) "St. Joseph River (Lake Michigan)") during the festival, including volleyball tournaments, a river run & walk, and sand sculpturing.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-40) The Lighted Boat Parade and the Classic Boat Display both took place along the St. Joseph River and were a part of the Venetian Festival since 1987. [Fireworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireworks "Fireworks") and rides were also attractions, bringing people from bigger cities such as [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"). A [blessing of the river](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blessing_of_the_river?action=edit&redlink=1 "Blessing of the river (page does not exist)") was done July 30, and continues as a tradition to this day.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Michigan#cite_note-41)

## Media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=St._Joseph,_Michigan&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Media")]

Saint Joseph is served by _[The Herald-Palladium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Herald-Palladium "The Herald-Palladium")_ newspaper, whose offices are in nearby [St. Joseph Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_Charter_Township,_Michigan "St. Joseph Charter Township, Michigan"). It is part of the [South Bend/Elkhart television market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:South_Bend_TV "Template:South Bend TV"), and is served by sister radio stations [WCSY-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WCSY-FM "WCSY-FM"), [WCXT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WCXT "WCXT"), [WIRX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WIRX "WIRX"), [WQYQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WQYQ "WQYQ"), [WRRA-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WRRA-FM "WRRA-FM"), and [WSJM-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSJM-FM "WSJM-FM"), as well as some in the [South Bend market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:South_Bend_Radio "Template:South Bend Radio").
